# Appearance

Change how the shell and the windows look, one setting at a time. Each change acts at once, is remembered, and can be shown first with `--dry-run`. For colors, see [Themes](/customize/themes/index.html).

## Try it

```bash
bxrig appearance bar layout minimal       # minimal, standard (the default), dense, status
bxrig appearance dock off                 # on, off, toggle
bxrig appearance font cascadia            # the coding font
bxrig appearance background random        # or: list, set NAME, next
```

![The coding fonts and Inter](/assets/screenshots/font-specimen.webp)

`bxrig appearance status` shows what you have chosen, and `bxrig appearance apply` pushes it all again. The menu has all of this under Appearance.

## Pick a bar

`bxrig appearance bar layout` picks one of three bars. Standard is the default. They all end with quick settings and then the control center, and they use bare icons coloured by the theme: only the logo button and the Launchpad grid carry a plate (a tile with an outline, so it stays visible on dark and Retro bars).

|  Layout  |              Start              |        Center         |                                                                          End                                                                           |
|----------|---------------------------------|-----------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Minimal  | logo, workspaces, active window | clock                 | tray, network, volume, battery\*, notifications, quick settings, control center                                                                        |
| Standard | logo, workspaces, active window | clock, media          | agents, capture, system, developer, VPN, tray, clipboard history, network, Bluetooth, volume, battery\*, notifications, quick settings, control center |
| Dense    | as Standard                     | clock, weather, media | as Standard, plus brightness                                                                                                                           |

\* The battery widget is written only when a battery is found (a laptop). It shows the percentage; `appearance battery-percent off` hides the number.

What each layout holds, in short:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["Minimal"] --> B["Logo, workspaces, clock, tray, status icons"]
  C["Standard"] --> D["Minimal plus media, agents, capture, system, developer, VPN, clipboard, Bluetooth"]
  E["Dense"] --> F["Standard plus weather and brightness"]
```

## Change the dock, windows and layout

```bash
bxrig appearance dock mode autohide       # always, autohide, off
bxrig appearance windows gaps off         # no gaps and no borders
bxrig appearance windows corners sharp    # theme, rounded, sharp
bxrig appearance windows opacity glassy   # opaque, glassy
bxrig appearance animations off
bxrig appearance layout columns           # dwindle, master, columns, scrolling, monocle, floating
bxrig appearance windows snap off         # floating windows stop snapping to edges (on by default)
```

## Change the fonts

```bash
bxrig appearance font list
bxrig appearance font install cascadia --yes
bxrig appearance font cascadia            # the coding font: terminals (and the shell, until you pick an interface font)
bxrig appearance ui-font inter            # the interface font: bar, panels and GTK apps
bxrig appearance font-rendering smooth    # default, smooth, crisp, sharp
```

Fonts are in three parts, also on the Look page of the Control Center (Fonts):

* **Coding font** , one of fifteen Nerd Fonts (`appearance font list`). JetBrains Mono is the default. Geist Mono, Monaspace Neon, IBM Plex Mono, Commit Mono and Atkinson Hyperlegible Mono (made for low vision) are new. Changing it updates the terminal configs BxRig wrote, but never one you edited (it tells you which).
* **Interface font** (`appearance ui-font list`): Inter, Noto Sans or IBM Plex Sans, for the bar, the panels and GTK apps. Inter is made for screens and is the closest to the Mac's system font. Until you pick one the shell uses the coding font. Plasma keeps its own font (System Settings \> Text \& Fonts).
* **Rendering** : `smooth` (no hinting, the Mac look, best on HiDPI), `crisp` (slight hinting, sharper on 1x screens), `sharp` (full hinting and subpixel, for low-resolution LCDs) or `default` (your distribution's). BxRig writes `~/.config/fontconfig/conf.d/60-bxrig-rendering.conf` and GTK's hinting settings; `default` removes the file unless you edited it. Open apps pick it up when they restart.

## Change the background

Backgrounds are read from `~/Pictures/BxRig`, `~/Pictures` and the current theme's folder.

The menu has all of this under Appearance.

## Icons

BxRig has its own icon theme, **BxRig** : superellipse tiles with a vertical glow and a white Phosphor duotone glyph, one color per kind (develop green, system blue, look purple, control indigo, utility amber). It covers what BxRig itself owns: the BxRig laptop and the app grid, the Develop, System and Look folders, the Setup Wizard, Runner menu, Control Center, About, and one icon for every page of `bxrig tui list`. Everything else is Papirus-Dark: the theme inherits it (`Inherits=Papirus-Dark,hicolor`), so apps look as they do in Papirus.

![The BxRig icons at 16 to 128 px](/assets/bxrig-icon-theme.png)

| ![The XFCE application menu with the BxRig folder open](/assets/screenshots/icons-xfce-menu.webp) **The application menu** (XFCE) | ![Rofi as an icon grid with the BxRig launchers](/assets/screenshots/icons-launcher-grid.webp) **A launcher grid** (Rofi) |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

```bash
bxrig appearance icons status
bxrig appearance icons bxrig --yes     # the default after `bxrig init` / setup: BxRig icons over Papirus-Dark
bxrig appearance icons papirus --yes   # Papirus-Dark alone; the BxRig launchers use the stock names again
```

The icon set is not a question in the wizard: setup applies `bxrig`, and this command switches later. It installs `papirus-icon-theme` (Arch `extra`, in the default tier of the catalog) when Papirus-Dark is missing, writes the theme to `~/.local/share/icons/BxRig`, and sets GTK (gsettings, the settings.ini line when the file has one, xfconf on XFCE), Qt (`qt6ct.conf`, and Plasma's icon theme), and the runner (Rofi, Fuzzel and Wofi through `bxrig runner icon-theme`). The application-menu launchers (`bxrig launchers on`) are rewritten to follow it. It writes files, so without `--yes` it prints the plan (exit 2). The glyphs are [Phosphor Icons](https://phosphoricons.com) (MIT); the licence is installed with the theme.

A theme-less icon name never leaves a gap: with `papirus`, or when an older BxRig has no theme installed, the launchers and the runner menu use the stock Papirus names (`applications-development`, `system-run`) and the plain `bxrig` icon.

## Where the changes go

Where each kind of setting ends up:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["bxrig appearance"] --> B["Noctalia: config-set or config.toml"]
  A --> C["Hyprland: look.lua"]
  A --> D["Fonts: fontconfig and GTK"]
```

* **Noctalia** (bar position and style, dock mode and position, battery, font, corner radius) is changed with `noctalia msg config-set`, so your `config.toml` is not edited. Without Noctalia the choice is saved and `appearance apply` pushes it later.
* **Hyprland** window looks (gaps, corners, opacity, animations, layout) are one generated file, `~/.config/bxrig/theme/look.lua`, loaded by `bxrig.lua`. BxRig reloads Hyprland after a change. Your own `hyprland.lua` is never touched.

These five settings (`bar layout`, `dock on|off|toggle`, `appgrid`, `battery-percent`, `time format`) rewrite `~/.config/noctalia/config.toml` through the config service: the theme and wallpaper you have are kept, a backup is made, and a running Noctalia reloads the file. If the file has changes of your own, the command shows a plan and `--yes` replaces it (the backup keeps yours). Noctalia's own settings window stores its changes separately and wins over the file; if the bar does not follow a change, look at `~/.local/state/noctalia/settings.toml`. The plate images are written to `~/.local/share/bxrig/plates/`. Noctalia's own first-run wizard is turned off in this config.

## Advanced

### Every setting

```bash
bxrig appearance status
bxrig appearance bar position bottom      # top, bottom, left, right
bxrig appearance bar style glassy         # opaque, glassy, clear
bxrig appearance bar clock iso            # ten clock formats (time-24h, sunday-12h, date-24h, iso ...)
bxrig appearance bar battery on           # the percentage next to the battery
bxrig appearance bar layout minimal       # minimal, standard (the default), dense, status
bxrig appearance dock off                 # on, off, toggle, status: the grid button moves between the dock and the bar
bxrig appearance appgrid launchpad        # launchpad, terminal, status
bxrig appearance battery-percent on       # laptops only
bxrig time format "%a %-I:%M %p"          # the bar clock's text; default "%b %-d - %H:%M" reads Nov 5 - 04:00
bxrig appearance dock mode autohide       # always, autohide, off
bxrig appearance windows gaps off         # no gaps and no borders
bxrig appearance windows corners sharp    # theme, rounded, sharp
bxrig appearance windows opacity glassy   # opaque, glassy
bxrig appearance animations off
bxrig appearance layout columns           # dwindle, master, columns, scrolling, monocle, floating
bxrig appearance windows snap off         # floating windows stop snapping to edges (on by default)
bxrig appearance font list
bxrig appearance font install cascadia --yes
bxrig appearance font cascadia            # the coding font: terminals (and the shell, until you pick an interface font)
bxrig appearance ui-font inter            # the interface font: bar, panels and GTK apps
bxrig appearance font-rendering smooth    # default, smooth, crisp, sharp
bxrig appearance background random        # or: list, set NAME, next
bxrig appearance apply                    # push everything you chose again
bxrig appearance icons papirus --yes      # the icon set: bxrig (default), papirus, status
```

### The bar's widgets in detail

* **Logo** opens the BxRig menu (`bxrig menu`). **Clock** is one widget: the time as text, a popover with your local time, the other zones you follow (`bxrig time world`) and a Calendar button; right click opens the Noctalia calendar.
* **Developer** (a code glyph, Standard and Dense) shows how many databases, containers and VMs are running. Its popover has three tabs: Databases (`bxrig db`), Containers (`bxrig containers`, over Podman or the engine `db engine` chose) and VMs (`bxrig vm`). Each row has a state dot, the host ports, start and stop (stop asks for a second click), a copy button for the connection string or address, and a logs button that opens `bxrig containers logs NAME` in a terminal; the footer opens the Machines page of `bxrig tui`. It refreshes every 15 seconds while open and every 2 minutes for the number.
* **Dock** is on by default. The Launchpad grid is its first button, so the grid is not in the bar; with `dock off` the grid button returns to the bar, right after the logo.
* **Quick settings** (`bxrig/quick`, the sliders icon) is a popover of switches and pickers: Caffeine, Do Not Disturb, Dark/Light/Auto, Dock, Battery percentage (laptops), App grid style, Top bar layout, Clock format, a button to the control center Home tile for Night light, and a button that opens the BxRig Control Center. Its **Themes** row opens the theme switcher (search, preview, Enter applies). Every control runs the matching bxrig command with `--yes` and shows its result. Caffeine is a switch here, not a bar icon: Noctalia can switch it (`noctalia msg caffeine-enable|disable`) but cannot report its state, so the switch shows what you last set in the popover.
* **Battery and power are one panel.** The battery is Noctalia's built-in widget (laptops only). A left click opens the BxRig **Power** panel (`bxrig/power`, a panel without a bar widget of its own); a right click opens the control center Power tab. The panel shows the charge, state, time remaining, watts, health and cycles, the power profile (Saver, Balanced, Performance), what closing the lid does on battery and on AC, Suspend and Hibernate (each asks first; Hibernate is greyed out with the reason until swap and resume are ready), and a charge limit slider when the battery supports it. It refreshes every 15 seconds while open. The lid and charge limit changes need sudo, so the panel runs them in a terminal window where the password is asked. The separate power profile widget is not on the bar.
* **System** (`bxrig/system`, a monitor glyph) shows the number of waiting updates beside it, hidden when there are none. Its popover has two tabs. **Updates** lists the repository and AUR packages (`bxrig system updates`), warns when a restart is needed (a kernel, systemd or glibc update, or a kernel that was already replaced), and **Update all** opens a terminal that runs `bxrig system update --yes`, so you see the snapshot that comes first and the progress. **Backups** shows a row for config snapshots, system snapshots and your files with the last run, the next run, the size and a health mark (`bxrig backup status`); **Back up now** and **Open Time Machine** run in a terminal too. The count is read every 10 minutes in the background and every minute while the popover is open.
* **VPN** (`bxrig/vpn`, a shield, Standard and Dense) is one list of every VPN you can use: the saved NetworkManager VPN and WireGuard profiles and the VPN apps (NordVPN, NordLayer, Tailscale, Mullvad). The shield is green while one is connected and grey otherwise, and hides itself when no VPN is installed. Switching one on disconnects the one that is connected, unless you turn on "Allow more than one at the same time" (`bxrig vpn set allow_several=true --yes`). A pin button picks a country or exit node. The same list is `bxrig vpn list`.
* **App grid** : `launchpad` is the launcher's grid view. `terminal` (a Terminal-style grid) is only remembered for now: nothing draws it yet, so the launcher keeps the Launchpad grid.
* **Clock format** uses Noctalia's date format tokens (<https://docs.noctalia.dev/noctalia/configuration/date-format-tokens/>). A pattern without a `%`, like `MMM d - HH:mm`, is read as letters (yyyy MM dd HH mm ss a ...) and converted.

### Text in large letters

`bxrig ascii` draws text in large letters with FIGlet fonts, the way `figlet` does, and paints it with a colour or a gradient. The BxRig logo is drawn the same way, in DOS Rebel.

```bash
bxrig ascii BxRig                                  # DOS Rebel, the brand gradient
bxrig ascii Hello --font=ansi-shadow --gradient=sunset
bxrig ascii OK --font=calvin-s --color=#00ff78     # small letters, one colour
bxrig ascii Deploy --gradient=#ff5f6d,#ffc371,#00dbff --direction=diagonal
bxrig ascii Theme --gradient=theme                 # your theme's accent colours
echo "build ok" | bxrig ascii                      # the text from stdin
bxrig ascii fonts                                  # every font, in its own name
```

* **Fonts:** `dos-rebel` (the default, 8 rows), `ansi-shadow` (6 rows) and `calvin-s` (3 rows, for narrow terminals). They ship inside BxRig, so nothing is installed.
* **`--color`:** `#rrggbb`, `#rgb`, `theme` (your theme's accent) or a name: black, white, gray, red, orange, yellow, green, cyan, blue, purple, magenta, pink, boxlang, bxrig.
* **`--gradient`:** a preset (`brand`, `theme`, `sunset`, `ocean`, `fire`, `forest`, `candy`, `rainbow`) or your own two or more colours separated by commas. `--direction` runs it `horizontal` (the default), `vertical` or `diagonal`.
* **When it colours:** without `--color` or `--gradient` you get the brand gradient in a terminal and plain text in a pipe or file. `--color` and `--gradient` colour even in a pipe. `--plain` and the `NO_COLOR` variable always give plain text.
* `--json` returns the lines, the font and the size.

#### Pictures as text

`bxrig ascii image` draws a PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP or SVG in the terminal. BxRig reads it with the [bx-image](https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/bx-image) module, which is built into the binary, so there is nothing to install.

```bash
bxrig ascii image ~/Pictures/logo.png              # 48 columns, half blocks in full colour
bxrig ascii image logo.svg --width=80              # SVGs are drawn at the size you ask for, so they stay sharp
bxrig ascii image photo.jpg --style=ascii          # characters from a brightness ramp, in the picture's colours
```

* **`--style`:** `blocks` (the default) uses half blocks, two pixels per row in 24-bit colour. `ascii` uses one character per cell (`.:-=+*#%@`), coloured like the picture.
* **`--width`:** 4 to 300 columns; the height follows the picture's shape. Transparent pixels stay blank.
* Colour follows the same rules as text: on in a terminal, off in a pipe, with `--plain` or with `NO_COLOR`. `--json` returns the lines without colour.

### About this rig

`bxrig about` shows the BxRig laptop, with BX in DOS Rebel on its screen, beside three panels drawn by [fastfetch](https://github.com/fastfetch-cli/fastfetch):

* **rig:** host, CPU, GPU, memory, disk and display
* **stack:** BoxLang and MatchBox, Java, Node and pnpm, Git and gh, your editor
* **look:** OS, desktop, theme, shell and terminal

Under the laptop: *BXRIG powered by BoxLang* and [www.boxlang.io](http://www.boxlang.io). Open it from the BxRig menu (**About** ), from the **BxRig About** launcher, or in any terminal:

```bash
bxrig about            # in your terminal
bxrig about --plain    # no colour
bxrig about --json     # version, theme and links as data
```

* **It follows your theme.** `bxrig theme set` redraws the laptop in the theme's colours (`~/.config/bxrig/theme/fastfetch-logo.ans`), and the panel labels use your terminal colours.
* **Plain `fastfetch` works too.** `bxrig setup shell` installs fastfetch and writes `~/.config/fastfetch/config.jsonc` once. After that it is yours to change; `bxrig about` keeps using its own copy in `~/.config/bxrig/fastfetch.jsonc`.
* Without fastfetch, `bxrig about` shows the laptop, the version and a hint to install it.

Next: [Accessibility](/customize/accessibility/index.html), [Boxy's look and voice](/customize/boxy-look/index.html), [Shortcuts](/desktop/shortcuts/index.html).

markdown:
# Backups and BxTimeMachine

Use this page to protect your setup, your system and your files, and to browse every backup on one timeline.

## Try it

```bash
bxrig backup status          # one line per kind: health, last run, next run, size
bxrig timemachine            # every backup on one timeline
bxrig backup config now      # a snapshot of your BxRig setup, right now
```

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["My BxRig setup"] --> A1["Config snapshots (BxRig)"]
  B["The whole system"] --> B1["snapper on Btrfs, Timeshift elsewhere"]
  C["My files"] --> C1["restic, encrypted"]
  C1 --> D["NAS, disk or cloud"]
  A1 --> C1
  A1 --> T["BxTimeMachine timeline"]
  B1 --> T
  C1 --> T
```

The diagram shows the three layers and that BxTimeMachine shows them together. Config snapshots also travel with your files, so any place protects them too.

|        Layer         |                                         What it keeps                                         |                       Tool                       |
|----------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| **My BxRig setup**   | Your settings, config files and package list, a small snapshot you can restore in one command | BxRig itself                                     |
| **The whole system** | Snapshots of the system before and after every update                                         | snapper on Btrfs, Timeshift on other filesystems |
| **My files**         | Projects, Documents and your SSH config, encrypted                                            | restic, to a NAS, a disk or the cloud            |

Everything shows a plan first and needs `--yes`. The setup wizard has a **NAS** page and a **Backups** page (local layers, backup apps and the copy somewhere else together).

## See the status

```bash
bxrig backup status
bxrig backup status --json   # the same as data (the System panel in the bar reads it)
```

There is one row for each kind of backup: **config** snapshots, **system** snapshots (snapper) and **files** (restic). Each shows when it last ran, when it runs next (from its timer, or "before the next update" for config snapshots), its size (known for config snapshots only) and a health:

| Health |                                Meaning                                 |
|--------|------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `ok`   | The newest backup is within the limit and the last run did not fail.   |
| `warn` | It is older than the limit, the last run failed, or restic is missing. |
| `none` | Nothing to judge yet: not set up, or never run.                        |

There is no separate "back up now" command: the row's own command does it, `backup config now`, `backup snapshots create --yes` or `backup data run --all --yes` (the JSON says which in `action`).

## Browse the timeline

```bash
bxrig timemachine          # every backup on one timeline
bxrig timemachine --local  # skip the network places so it opens at once
bxrig timemachine --demo   # made-up data, nothing runs
```

Places are rows (system, config, each place your files go to, plain NAS copies) and time runs left to right, newest on the right. Points are coloured by how old they are (hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, yearly). The backup you choose is a card with older ones stacked behind it. Open one to browse its files, filter them, restore, export or send it to another place. Every change shows its plan first and runs only when you press `y`. Press `?` for the keys.

## Back up and restore your BxRig setup

```bash
bxrig backup config now
bxrig backup config list
bxrig backup config diff 20261113T153000
bxrig backup config restore 20261113T153000 --dry-run
bxrig backup config restore 20261113T153000 --only=.config/hypr --yes
```

A snapshot is taken by itself before `update apply`, `system update`, `init`, `reinstall` and `refresh` (turn it off with `backup config auto off`). Restoring takes a safety snapshot of the present first. Secrets and SSH keys are never in a snapshot unless you add `--with-secrets`, which stores your secrets export, encrypted with a passphrase you type. `backup export config ID --to=FILE` writes a snapshot as one file to carry to another machine.

## Snapshot the whole system

```bash
bxrig backup snapshots setup --yes     # snapper, 5 hourly, 7 daily, 2 weekly, 1 monthly; one before and after every pacman update
bxrig backup snapshots list
bxrig backup snapshots restore 12 /home/me/projects/app --dry-run
```

There is no automatic whole-system rollback: how to roll back a Btrfs root depends on how your subvolumes are laid out. Boot the snapshot from the boot menu and follow the Arch wiki's snapper page, or restore folders with `restore`.

## Back up your files

A **place** is where a restic repository lives. Add one, create it, back up, and schedule it:

```bash
bxrig backup data target add spaces --type=s3 --endpoint=https://nyc3.digitaloceanspaces.com --bucket=mybackups --ask-keys
bxrig backup data init spaces --yes
bxrig backup data run --all --yes
bxrig backup data schedule daily --yes
```

Access keys are typed hidden and go to your keyring; the repository password is made for you and kept there too, so keep a copy (`bxrig secrets get BXRIG_BACKUP_SPACES_PASSWORD --show`).
> **Warning:** Losing the repository password loses the backups. Keep a copy somewhere safe.

The schedule is a user timer: it skips on battery power, catches up after the computer was off, and tells you when a backup fails. `backup data restore ID --to=DIR` restores into a folder you name, never over your files by itself. `backup send ID --from=PLACE --to=PLACE` copies a snapshot to a second place (a NAS and the cloud, for a 3-2-1 setup), and `backup export data ID --to=FILE.zip` writes one as an archive.

To keep files on a NAS, see [Your NAS](/data/nas/index.html).

## Advanced

### Place types

`local` (a disk or folder), a NAS (see [Your NAS](/data/nas/index.html)), `sftp`, `rest`, `s3` (AWS, DigitalOcean Spaces, Wasabi, MinIO), `b2` (Backblaze), `azure`, `gs` (Google Cloud Storage) and `rclone` (FTP, WebDAV and anything rclone speaks, set up with `bxrig cloud configure`).

### Health limits

The limits are 30 days for config snapshots; 2 days for system snapshots while the snapper timeline timer is on (14 without it); and for files 6 hours with an hourly schedule, 2 days with a daily one and 14 days with none. The time of the last files backup is the one `backup data run` records for each place, so the status makes no network call. Timeshift keeps its own schedule and its last run is not read.

Next: [Your NAS](/data/nas/index.html) · [Scheduler](/data/scheduler/index.html) · [Move to another machine](/data/export-import/index.html)

markdown:
# Developer tools

Use this page to install the tools around your code and to check that your developer setup is complete.

## Try it

```bash
bxrig doctor --dev
bxrig git signing on --yes
bxrig pkg install bruno --yes
```

## Check your setup

```bash
bxrig doctor --dev
```

After the usual tool checks, `--dev` looks at your git name and email, the SSH key, the SSH agent, commit signing, a container engine and `EDITOR`. Each one that is missing prints `warn` with the command that fixes it. They are advice: the exit code stays 0.

## Sign your commits

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["SSH key"] --> B["bxrig git signing on"]
  B --> C["git signs commits and tags"]
  B --> D["allowed_signers file"]
  D --> E["git log shows verified"]
  A --> F["Add as Signing key on GitHub"]
  F --> G["Verified badge"]
```

The diagram shows what one SSH key does once signing is on.

```bash
bxrig git signing on --yes      # sign commits and tags with ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
bxrig git signing               # on or off, and with which key
bxrig git signing off --yes     # stop signing; the key stays
```

`on` uses your SSH key (no GPG). It sets `gpg.format ssh`, `user.signingkey`, `commit.gpgsign` and `tag.gpgsign`, and adds your email and key to `~/.config/git/allowed_signers`, so `git log --show-signature` can verify your own commits. It needs the key (`bxrig ssh key --yes`) and `git user.email`. `--key=PATH` picks another key.

For GitHub's Verified badge, add the same public key to GitHub a second time, as a **Signing key** (Settings, SSH and GPG keys).

![bxrig git signing: the plan, then on](/assets/screenshots/devtools-signing-plan.webp)

The setup wizard offers this after the SSH key ("Sign commits with that key").

## Install an API client

Postman, Insomnia and Bruno are in the app picker under Development \> API clients. On Arch they come from the AUR (`postman-bin`, `insomnia-bin`, `bruno-bin`); on Debian, Ubuntu and openSUSE from Flathub.

```bash
bxrig pkg install bruno --yes
```

Bruno keeps its collections as plain files in your project, so they go into git with the code.

## Install cloud and Kubernetes tools

The **Cloud and Kubernetes** profile installs kubectl, k9s, Helm and OpenTofu, and offers the AWS, Google Cloud and Azure CLIs.

![The cloud tools and API clients in the catalog](/assets/screenshots/devtools-catalog.webp)

A tool that is not packaged on your distribution is not offered there.

## Shell helpers

Two more in the picker, under Development \> Shell:

* **atuin**: shell history you can search, with the directory and exit code of every command. It stays on your machine unless you sign in to sync.
* **just** : a `justfile` of project commands (`just test`, `just deploy`), simpler than make.

## Advanced

### Where each cloud tool comes from

|        Tool         |     Arch     |    Debian    |    Ubuntu    |       openSUSE        |
|---------------------|--------------|--------------|--------------|-----------------------|
| kubectl             | extra        | apt          | not packaged | `kubernetes-client`   |
| k9s, Helm, OpenTofu | extra        | not packaged | not packaged | zypper                |
| AWS CLI             | `aws-cli-v2` | `awscli`     | `awscli`     | `aws-cli` (version 1) |
| Google Cloud CLI    | AUR          | not packaged | not packaged | not packaged          |
| Azure CLI           | extra        | apt          | not packaged | zypper                |

Next: [BoxLang and MatchBox](/build/boxlang/index.html) · [Databases and virtual machines](/build/databases-and-vms/index.html) · [Security](/maintain/security/index.html)

# Files and folders

**Where the folders are.** One rule for every file BxRig writes: `BXRIG_CONFIG_HOME`, then `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, then `~/.config` for the config folder (the same for `BXRIG_STATE_HOME`/`XDG_STATE_HOME`, `XDG_DATA_HOME`, `XDG_CACHE_HOME`). If you set `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, everything below that says `~/.config` lives under it instead, including `bxrig/`, `menus/`, `nvim/` and `strata/`. `BXRIG_DATA_HOME` and `BXRIG_CACHE_HOME` name BxRig's own data and cache folder directly (default `~/.local/share/bxrig`, `~/.cache/bxrig`). The tests use these overrides. `BXRIG_APPS_DIRS` replaces the folders read for `.desktop` files.

|                                              Path                                               |                                                                           What                                                                           |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `~/.local/bin/bxrig`                                                                            | the program                                                                                                                                              |
| `~/.config/bxrig/answers.json`                                                                  | your wizard answers (mode 600, no secrets)                                                                                                               |
| `~/.config/bxrig/shortcuts.json`                                                                | your shortcut changes (`keys set`)                                                                                                                       |
| `~/.config/bxrig/keystyle.json`                                                                 | the shortcut style (`traditional` or `mac`), the keyboard (`pc` or `apple`) and the Alt/Win swap                                                         |
| `~/.config/xremap/config.yml`                                                                   | generated xremap remaps (Cmd-style keys, and the Alt/Win swap in the Mac style on a PC keyboard); never edit                                             |
| `~/.config/systemd/user/xremap.service`                                                         | runs xremap with that file                                                                                                                               |
| `~/.config/bxrig/runner.json`                                                                   | launcher and menu program                                                                                                                                |
| `~/.config/bxrig/update.json`                                                                   | update channel and notification setting                                                                                                                  |
| `~/.config/bxrig/skills.json`                                                                   | the agent skills BxRig installed                                                                                                                         |
| `~/.config/bxrig/appearance.json`                                                               | what you chose in `bxrig appearance` (bar layout, dock, app grid, battery percentage, clock format, windows, font)                                       |
| `~/.local/share/bxrig/plates/`                                                                  | the logo-button and Launchpad-grid plates (SVG and PNG) the Noctalia bar and dock point at                                                               |
| `~/.matchbox.env`                                                                               | your MatchBox environment variables (`bxrig boxlang matchbox env`, mode 600); a MatchBox with a runtime home reads it on every run                       |
| `~/.matchbox/config/boxlang.json`                                                               | the MatchBox runtime config (`bxrig boxlang matchbox log-level` changes `logging.rootLevel`); `MATCHBOX_HOME` moves the home                             |
| `~/.boxlang`                                                                                    | BoxLang's home: modules (`bxrig boxlang modules`), `config/boxlang.json` and logs; `BOXLANG_HOME` moves it (`bxrig boxlang home`)                        |
| `~/.config/bxrig/display.json`                                                                  | what you chose in `bxrig display` (scale, rotation, mirror, laptop panel)                                                                                |
| `~/.config/bxrig/theme.json`                                                                    | the current theme and mode                                                                                                                               |
| `~/.config/bxrig/theme/hypr.lua`                                                                | generated Hyprland border colours of the theme; never edit                                                                                               |
| `~/.config/bxrig/theme/look.lua`                                                                | generated Hyprland window looks (gaps, corners, opacity); never edit                                                                                     |
| `~/.config/bxrig/theme/monitors.lua`                                                            | generated Hyprland monitor settings; never edit                                                                                                          |
| `~/.config/bxrig/nas.json`                                                                      | your NAS boxes (no passwords)                                                                                                                            |
| `~/.config/bxrig/backup.json`                                                                   | backup places, what is backed up, retention, schedule (no keys)                                                                                          |
| `~/.local/share/bxrig/backups/config/`                                                          | your BxRig config snapshots                                                                                                                              |
| `/etc/bxrig/nas/NAME.cred`                                                                      | the SMB credentials of a NAS, root only (mode 600)                                                                                                       |
| `~/.config/systemd/user/bxrig-backup.{service,timer}`                                           | the automatic file backup                                                                                                                                |
| `~/.config/bxrig/vms/`                                                                          | one record per virtual machine                                                                                                                           |
| `/etc/systemd/logind.conf.d/50-bxrig-lid.conf`                                                  | what closing the lid does (`bxrig power lid`); remove it to go back to the defaults                                                                      |
| `/etc/pam.d/sudo` and `.bxrig-backup`                                                           | one marked line per `bxrig security fingerprint\|fido2 on`; the backup is the original                                                                   |
| `/etc/sudoers.d/50-bxrig-nopasswd`                                                              | passwordless sudo (`bxrig security passwordless-sudo on`)                                                                                                |
| `/etc/systemd/system/automatic-timezoned.service`, `/etc/geoclue/conf.d/90-bxrig-timezone.conf` | the automatic time zone (`bxrig time auto on`)                                                                                                           |
| `~/.config/bxrig/plasma-panels/`                                                                | the Plasma panel layout and its backup                                                                                                                   |
| `~/.config/bxrig/welcome.html`                                                                  | the getting-started page                                                                                                                                 |
| `~/.config/bxrig/agents.json`                                                                   | BoxLang agents: each project's port, the default agent, the projects folder when you changed it, projects added by path, the agents' skills you reviewed |
| `~/.config/systemd/user/bxrig-agent-NAME.service`                                               | one BoxLang agent running in the background (`bxrig ai agents start NAME`)                                                                               |
| `~/Agents/`                                                                                     | your BoxLang agent projects (`BXRIG_AGENTS_DIR` or `bxrig ai agents dir PATH` moves it)                                                                  |
| `~/.bxagents/Agent.yml`                                                                         | bx-agents' settings for all your agents; BxRig writes only its marked `bxrig` profile block (`BXAGENTS_USER_CONFIG` names another file)                  |
| `~/.bxagents/NAME/`                                                                             | each agent's data (chats, notes, files, skills, logs): bx-agents' own default                                                                            |
| `~/.config/hypr/bxrig.lua`                                                                      | generated Hyprland module (never edit); `hyprland.lua` is yours                                                                                          |
| `~/.agents/skills/`                                                                             | the agent skills store, linked into each agent                                                                                                           |
| `~/.config/systemd/user/bxrig-*.service`                                                        | night shift, AirPlay, update check, cloud mounts                                                                                                         |
| `~/.cache/bxrig/install.log`                                                                    | the installer's log                                                                                                                                      |
| `~/Videos/bxrig-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.mp4`                                                            | screen recordings (`bxrig record`; `BXRIG_VIDEOS` changes the folder)                                                                                    |

Every file BxRig writes goes through one safe writer: atomic replace, a backup, a journal, and a **drift** check. A file you changed is kept and reported as drifted. `bxrig config diff NAME` shows how it differs from what BxRig would write.

title: Install
body: Install One command turns a fresh Linux install into your dev rig. It takes a few minutes and asks once. curl -fsSL {{ installUrl }} | bash Before you start You need Notes A supported distribution CachyOS, Arch Linux, openSUSE Tumbleweed or Slowroll, Ubuntu 26.04 LTS or Debian 13. See Distributions . x86_64 hardware Other architectures are not supported. A normal user with sudo The installer refuses to run as root. A network connection Everything is downloaded and verified on the way. What happens flowchart LR A["Check the machine"] --> B["Download and verify the release"] B --> C["Install packages and toolchains"] C --> D["Install the core apps"] D --> E["Setup wizard"] E --> F["Your rig"] Check. It looks at your distribution and shows you the plan, then asks once. Download and verify. The program and the install bundle for your channel are checked against a signature and a SHA-256 before anything is installed. See Security . Install. Tip: The install log is ~/.cache/bxrig/install.log . Send it when you ask for help. When it is done You land in the wizard. When it ends, try the first hour . # Install

One command turns a fresh Linux install into your dev rig. It takes a few minutes and asks once.

```bash
curl -fsSL {{ installUrl }} | bash
```

![The setup wizard starts when the install is done](/assets/screenshots/wizard-welcome.webp)

## Before you start

|         You need          |                                                                   Notes                                                                    |
|---------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| A supported distribution  | CachyOS, Arch Linux, openSUSE Tumbleweed or Slowroll, Ubuntu 26.04 LTS or Debian 13. See [Distributions](/start/distributions/index.html). |
| x86_64 hardware           | Other architectures are not supported.                                                                                                     |
| A normal user with `sudo` | The installer refuses to run as root.                                                                                                      |
| A network connection      | Everything is downloaded and verified on the way.                                                                                          |

## What happens

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Check the machine"] --> B["Download and verify the release"]
    B --> C["Install packages and toolchains"]
    C --> D["Install the core apps"]
    D --> E["Setup wizard"]
    E --> F["Your rig"]
```

1. **Check.** It looks at your distribution and shows you the plan, then asks once.
2. **Download and verify.** The program and the install bundle for your [channel](/maintain/updates/index.html) are checked against a signature and a SHA-256 before anything is installed. See [Security](/maintain/security/index.html).
3. **Install.** Packages, then the toolchains (Java 21, `bvm`, `mvm`, BoxLang, MatchBox, Rust) and the core apps.
4. **Wizard.** The [setup wizard](/start/wizard/index.html) asks for your choices and shows exactly what it will run before it does.

> **Tip:** The install log is `~/.cache/bxrig/install.log`. Send it when you ask for help.

## When it is done

You land in the wizard. When it ends, try the [first hour](/start/first-hour/index.html).

|         Do this         |               With                |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| See what is set up      | `bxrig status`                    |
| Change your choices     | `bxrig init`                      |
| Open the control center | `Super+Alt+Space` or `bxrig menu` |
| See every shortcut      | `Super+K` or `bxrig keys sheet`   |
| Check for updates       | `bxrig update check`              |

## Other ways to install

Unattended installs, the beta channel, a specific MatchBox or a branch you want to test are on [Install options](/start/install-advanced/index.html). Something went wrong? See [Troubleshooting](/start/troubleshooting/index.html).

## Next

* [Your first hour](/start/first-hour/index.html)
* [The setup wizard](/start/wizard/index.html)

# Local AI

Use this page to run AI models on your own machine. BxRig looks at your hardware, offers the models that fit, downloads them, checks that they answer, and serves them all from one server. Nothing leaves your machine.

## Try it

```bash
bxrig ai setup --yes              # the balanced pick and the embedding model
bxrig ai ask "What is BoxLang?"
bxrig ai status                   # hardware, engine, server, active model, models
```

![The AI page of the Control Center](/assets/screenshots/ai-page-model.webp)

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["Your hardware"] --> B["Picks that fit"]
  B --> C["Download and verify"]
  C --> D["llama.cpp server 127.0.0.1:8089"]
  D --> E["Agents and apps"]
  D --> F["bxrig ai ask"]
```

The diagram shows the path from your hardware to a model that apps and agents can call.

## Set it up

The wizard asks on its AI page (now or later). Later works the same way:

```bash
bxrig ai setup                    # the plan: engine, models, server
bxrig ai setup --yes              # the balanced pick and the embedding model
bxrig ai setup --picks=all --tune --yes
```

`setup` installs llama.cpp when it is missing, downloads the models, starts the server, asks each model a test question and, with `--tune`, tunes them for your machine.

## Use it from your apps

Any app or agent that speaks one of these APIs can use your models:

|                API                |                Address                |
|-----------------------------------|---------------------------------------|
| OpenAI (chat, completions, tools) | `http://127.0.0.1:8089/v1`            |
| Anthropic (messages)              | `http://127.0.0.1:8089/v1/messages`   |
| Embeddings                        | `http://127.0.0.1:8089/v1/embeddings` |

## See what fits

```bash
bxrig ai hardware
bxrig ai models recommend          # up to three picks for this machine
bxrig ai models recommend --all    # everything that fits
```

BxRig works out a **budget** for models: the memory of a dedicated graphics card minus 1 GB, or half of your RAM when the graphics share it. From the budget it offers up to three chat models:

|            Pick            |                         What it is                         |
|----------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------|
| **balanced** (the default) | the best score among models that answer in about 3 seconds |
| **fastest**                | the quickest model that still does well                    |
| **capable**                | the best score that fits                                   |

Each model in BxRig's catalog was tested by BxRig on 20 tasks (following instructions, tool calls, JSON, reasoning); the score is shown next to it. Models BxRig has not tested are listed with `--all` but never picked. A small embedding model (EmbeddingGemma 300M) comes with every setup, for search over your own files.

## Get, switch and test models

```bash
bxrig ai models                    # what you have, the active one marked
bxrig ai models pull gemma-4-e4b qwen3.5-0.8b --yes
bxrig ai models use qwen3.5-0.8b   # the active chat model
bxrig ai models test               # ask each one a question, timed
bxrig ai models tune --yes         # benchmark threads, batch size, flash attention
bxrig ai models remove qwen3.5-0.8b --yes
```

Downloads run up to three at a time, continue where they stopped after an interruption, and are checked against the checksum in BxRig's catalog before they are used. A file that does not match is kept as `.part` and never served.

**Tune** runs llama.cpp's benchmark on each model (about a minute) with different thread counts, batch sizes and flash attention, and keeps the fastest settings for your machine. You can skip it at setup and run it any time.

## Discover more models

```bash
bxrig ai discover                  # staff picks for this machine, then the most downloaded GGUF models
bxrig ai discover qwen --fits      # search Hugging Face; only what fits here
bxrig ai models pull hf:bartowski/SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct-GGUF --yes
```

**Staff picks** are the models BxRig tested, picked for your hardware. The rest come from Hugging Face and are marked as not tested by BxRig. For each repository BxRig picks one file (a 4-bit quant first), shows its size and whether it fits, and checks the download against the SHA-256 that Hugging Face publishes. Only language models are listed (text, text with images, embeddings).

## Download in the background

```bash
bxrig ai models pull gemma-4-e4b qwen3.5-4b --background --yes
bxrig ai downloads                 # each one's share, queued, checking, done or failed
bxrig ai downloads cancel qwen3.5-4b
bxrig ai downloads clear           # forget the finished ones
```

Three download at a time; the rest wait in the queue. A background pull keeps going when you close the terminal or the Control Center.

## Work on selected text

Select text anywhere and press **Super+Alt+E**: a menu offers Summarize, Rewrite clearly, Fix spelling and grammar, Explain, Translate and Draft a reply. The result is copied to the clipboard and shown in a notification.

```bash
bxrig ai text summarize                      # the selection, else the clipboard
bxrig ai text translate --lang=Spanish
bxrig ai text fix --text="teh cat" --to=stdout
bxrig ai text menu
```

## Point coding agents at your model

```bash
bxrig ai link                              # which agents use the local server
bxrig ai link opencode --yes               # add BxRig's server to OpenCode
bxrig ai link opencode --default --yes     # and make the active model its default
bxrig ai link crush --yes
bxrig ai link opencode --off --yes
```

Only BxRig's own part of each agent's config is written (a provider called `bxrig`); everything else stays, and the old file is kept as `.bxrig-backup`. OpenCode gets a provider in `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` with your chat models; Crush gets a `llamacpp` provider block in `~/.config/crush/crushrc` and finds the models itself. A config with comments (JSONC) is not rewritten. While the server listens on your network it needs an API key, so agents are linked only while it listens on 127.0.0.1.

## In the Control Center and the bar

The **AI** page of the Control Center (`bxrig tui ai`) shows your machine, the engine, the server, your models and the picks you do not have yet. `Enter` downloads a pick or makes a model active, `t` tests, `u` tunes, `h` opens the model on Hugging Face, `x` removes it, `p` asks a question and `s` sets everything up.

**Discover** (`bxrig tui ai-discover`) shows downloads in progress, the staff picks and Hugging Face: `/` searches, `Enter` queues a download, `c` cancels one, `h` opens the model on Hugging Face. **Agents** (`bxrig tui ai-agents`) lists your coding agents: the default one, which use the local server (`l` switches), their sessions; `Enter` starts a session and `d` makes one the default. On the AI page, `b` runs the bench on the model under the cursor.

The bar's Agents panel has a **Local** tab: the server with Start and Stop, your models with Use, downloads in progress, and a box to try a question.

## Advanced

### The engine

```bash
bxrig ai engine                    # installed? which build?
bxrig ai engine install --yes      # the official installer (llama.app)
bxrig ai engine install --source=aur --yes   # Arch: llama.cpp-vulkan-bin
bxrig ai engine update --yes
```

The official installer checks your machine and installs the matching build: CUDA on NVIDIA, ROCm on AMD cards, Vulkan for other graphics, or the CPU build. It goes to `~/.local/bin/llama`.

### The server

```bash
bxrig ai serve                     # running? where?
bxrig ai serve start
bxrig ai serve stop
bxrig ai serve --listen=0.0.0.0 --yes   # also on your network
```

The server is a user service (`bxrig-ai.service`) running llama.cpp in router mode: every model you downloaded is available by its id, loaded when it is first asked for. Listening on your network (`0.0.0.0`) needs an API key: BxRig makes one, shows it once and keeps it in `~/.config/bxrig/ai-api-key` (only you can read it). Send it as `Authorization: Bearer KEY`.

### How well a model does here

```bash
bxrig ai bench                     # the active model
bxrig ai bench qwen3.5-0.8b
```

`bench` runs BxRig's 20 tool-calling tasks (setting a theme, a reminder, an agenda, installing an app, two actions at once, and requests that need no tool) against your own server and reports the score, the median reply time and the tasks it missed. These are the same tasks behind the scores in BxRig's catalog, so you can compare a model you found on Hugging Face with the tested ones. The result is kept with the model and shown in `bxrig ai models`.

You can also pull a specific quant: `bxrig ai models pull hf:OWNER/REPO/FILE.gguf --yes`.

### Files

|                   File                    |                                     What it holds                                     |
|-------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `~/.local/share/bxrig/models/`            | the model files                                                                       |
| `~/.config/bxrig/ai.json`                 | your models, the active one, tuned settings, measured speed, where the server listens |
| `~/.config/bxrig/ai-models.ini`           | the server's model list, written from `ai.json`                                       |
| `~/.config/systemd/user/bxrig-ai.service` | the server                                                                            |
| `~/.local/state/bxrig/ai-downloads/`      | the download queue, one record per model                                              |

Other local AI apps (LM Studio, Jan, Ollama and others) are still in the app catalog if you prefer them.

Next: [BoxLang agents](/ai/boxlang-agents/index.html) · [MCP and privacy](/ai/mcp-and-privacy/index.html) · [AI agents and skills](/ai/agents/index.html)

A request context is created and the Application listener is resolved (section 3). The class is instantiated (its init is NOT special here; the constructor runs, pseudo-constructor included). If the instance has a main member ( this scope), run listener.onRequestStart(templatePath) . If it returns true, call main( args ) where args is an array of the raw CLI arguments after the file name , in order ( ["hola", "--many", "options=test"] ). main may be an instance or static method; args = [] default is the convention. Errors: abort -> onAbort ; missing include -> onMissingTemplate ; any other exception -> log, then onError(exception, "") , rethrown if onError is false. Always onRequestEnd(templatePath) and flush output. No main : error Class [X] does not have a main method to execute. (non-zero exit). A path without extension is presumed to be <path>.bx . CLIGetArgs() and server.cli.parsed work inside the class as in scripts. 2. Mappings The only ways to declare them (owner decision, matches the JVM): this.mappings in Application.bx . mappings in boxlang.json (runtime config; the JVM default is { "/": "${user-dir}" } ). The bx:application component, which merges all of its attributes into the application settings ( name , mappings , ...), then recomputes the request config. Value forms: a string path, or a struct { path, external } ( path required, external default true ; BoxLang 1.6+). Names are normalized to a leading and trailing slash ( models and /models/ are the same). Application mappings are merged over the global ones, application wins. Class resolution order ( BoxResolver.findFromLocal ): 1) relative to the current template, 2) mappings (a mapping matches when the class path, as a slash path, starts with the mapping name; one candidate per valid extension, .bx before .bxs as configured), 3) custom component/class paths. Applies to new , import , extends , implements and createObject("class", name) . 3. Application.bx for scripts and classes Discovery ( ApplicationService.loadDescriptorTemplate ): for an absolute script path, the descriptor is looked up in the script's directory only ; for non-absolute (mapped) paths it walks up from the template's directory to its mapping root. Lookup order in a directory: class files Application.bx (valid class extensions, then .cfc ), then templates Application.<template extension> . The class is instantiated without calling init() . Settings read from this : name , mappings , datasource / defaultDatasource / datasources , javaSettings , classPaths / componentPaths , customComponentPaths , caches , schedulers , watchers , timezone , locale , runtimeSettings , security extension lists. A settings change recomputes the request config. Lifecycle for a script or class run (no web scopes): application defined on first use -> onApplicationStart() once (only if this.name is set; false aborts) -> onRequestStart(targetPage) (false aborts) -> run the script ( template.invoke ; onRequest is not used for scripts) or main(args) -> onRequestEnd() -> flush. Errors go to onError(exception, eventName) ; abort to onAbort(targetPage) . onApplicationEnd(applicationScope) on shutdown. Session hooks never fire in CLI. 4. How BxRig uses them Class entry with main(args) in the interpreter and in the native binary: src/Main.bx . Mappings from this.mappings in Application.bx : the bxrig package, including the nested bxrig.util package; tests run from src/ so bxrig.X resolves, and .bxs tests find lib.Check next to the script. Application.bx lifecycle for the class run: onError turns an unexpected exception into exit 9. Native builds resolve classes at compile time, so the mapped directories must exist when matchbox --target native runs; the lifecycle runs inside the binary. A native build of the whole program does not fit in a 14 GB machine (see CODE-REVIEW.md , "Startup of the native binary"); the .bxs tests and the interpreter do. MatchBox VM fixes (PRs 156 to 160, in the bxrig branch) Found while building the installer, fixed upstream, and BxRig no longer works around them: break in nested for-in loops (#156), a broken pipe on stdout (#157), calling a function stored in variables (#158), switch with var slots and the default jump (#159), and the panic message that was hidden (#160). Behaviour change in #159: a var declared in one case is not visible in another case.

# MatchBox parity work: class entry, mappings, Application.bx

Source of truth: BoxLang JVM (`ortus-boxlang/boxlang`, read 2026-11-09 at b8ea0f0) and the BoxLang docs (CLI Scripting, Application.bx). The `bxrig` branch of MatchBox (0.14.0 in `box.json`) has all three and BxRig builds on them: `src/Main.bx` is the entry class (`main( args )`), `src/Application.bx` sets `this.mappings` (`/bxrig` to `src/bxrig`, so `new bxrig.util.Proc()` resolves) and `onError` (exit 9). Sections 1 to 3 are the JVM behaviour that was copied.

## 1. Class as entry point (`boxlang Task.bx a b`)

JVM: `BoxRuntime.executeTemplate` sends `.bx`/`.cfc` files to `executeClass`.

1. A request context is created and the Application listener is resolved (section 3).
2. The class is instantiated (its `init` is NOT special here; the constructor runs, pseudo-constructor included).
3. If the instance has a `main` member (`this` scope), run `listener.onRequestStart(templatePath)`. If it returns true, call `main( args )` where `args` is an **array of the raw CLI arguments after the file name** , in order (`["hola", "--many", "options=test"]`). `main` may be an instance or static method; `args = []` default is the convention.
4. Errors: abort -\> `onAbort`; missing include -\> `onMissingTemplate`; any other exception -\> log, then `onError(exception, "")`, rethrown if `onError` is false. Always `onRequestEnd(templatePath)` and flush output.
5. No `main`: error `Class [X] does not have a main method to execute.` (non-zero exit).
6. A path without extension is presumed to be `<path>.bx`. `CLIGetArgs()` and `server.cli.parsed` work inside the class as in scripts.

## 2. Mappings

The only ways to declare them (owner decision, matches the JVM):

* `this.mappings` in `Application.bx`.
* `mappings` in `boxlang.json` (runtime config; the JVM default is `{ "/": "${user-dir}" }`).
* The `bx:application` component, which merges all of its attributes into the application settings (`name`, `mappings`, ...), then recomputes the request config.

Value forms: a string path, or a struct `{ path, external }` (`path` required, `external` default `true`; BoxLang 1.6+). Names are normalized to a leading and trailing slash (`models` and `/models/` are the same). Application mappings are merged over the global ones, application wins.

Class resolution order (`BoxResolver.findFromLocal`): 1) relative to the current template, 2) mappings (a mapping matches when the class path, as a slash path, starts with the mapping name; one candidate per valid extension, `.bx` before `.bxs` as configured), 3) custom component/class paths. Applies to `new`, `import`, `extends`, `implements` and `createObject("class", name)`.

## 3. Application.bx for scripts and classes

Discovery (`ApplicationService.loadDescriptorTemplate`): for an absolute script path, the descriptor is looked up in **the script's directory only** ; for non-absolute (mapped) paths it walks up from the template's directory to its mapping root. Lookup order in a directory: class files `Application.bx` (valid class extensions, then `.cfc`), then templates `Application.<template extension>`. The class is instantiated **without calling `init()`**.

Settings read from `this`: `name`, `mappings`, `datasource`/`defaultDatasource`/`datasources`, `javaSettings`, `classPaths`/`componentPaths`, `customComponentPaths`, `caches`, `schedulers`, `watchers`, `timezone`, `locale`, `runtimeSettings`, security extension lists. A settings change recomputes the request config.

Lifecycle for a script or class run (no web scopes): application defined on first use -\> `onApplicationStart()` once (only if `this.name` is set; false aborts) -\> `onRequestStart(targetPage)` (false aborts) -\> run the script (`template.invoke`; `onRequest` is not used for scripts) or `main(args)` -\> `onRequestEnd()` -\> flush. Errors go to `onError(exception, eventName)`; `abort` to `onAbort(targetPage)`. `onApplicationEnd(applicationScope)` on shutdown. Session hooks never fire in CLI.

## 4. How BxRig uses them

1. Class entry with `main(args)` in the interpreter and in the native binary: `src/Main.bx`.
2. Mappings from `this.mappings` in `Application.bx`: the `bxrig` package, including the nested `bxrig.util` package; tests run from `src/` so `bxrig.X` resolves, and `.bxs` tests find `lib.Check` next to the script.
3. `Application.bx` lifecycle for the class run: `onError` turns an unexpected exception into exit 9.

Native builds resolve classes at compile time, so the mapped directories must exist when `matchbox --target native` runs; the lifecycle runs inside the binary. A native build of the whole program does not fit in a 14 GB machine (see `CODE-REVIEW.md`, "Startup of the native binary"); the `.bxs` tests and the interpreter do.

## MatchBox VM fixes (PRs 156 to 160, in the `bxrig` branch)

Found while building the installer, fixed upstream, and BxRig no longer works around them: `break` in nested for-in loops (#156), a broken pipe on stdout (#157), calling a function stored in `variables` (#158), `switch` with `var` slots and the default jump (#159), and the panic message that was hidden (#160). Behaviour change in #159: a `var` declared in one `case` is not visible in another case.

# Security

Use this page to know what BxRig checks before it changes your machine, and how to turn on a fingerprint or security key for `sudo`.

## Try it

```bash
bxrig security status
bxrig security fingerprint on --dry-run   # prints the exact PAM line first
```

## What is verified

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["CI signs version info and install.sh (Ed25519)"] --> B["Public key in the program and installer"]
  B --> C["Installer or bxrig update"]
  C --> D{"Signature and SHA-256 match?"}
  D -->|"yes"| E["Install or replace"]
  D -->|"no"| F["Stop, nothing changed"]
```

The diagram shows what happens at install and update time: nothing is applied unless the signature and checksums match.

* **Releases are signed.** CI signs each channel's `version-latest.properties` and `install.sh` with an Ed25519 key. The public key is built into the program and into the published installer. The installer and `bxrig update` verify the signature and the SHA-256 of every file they download; any mismatch stops before anything changes.
* **The first `curl | bash`** trusts the script it downloads (TLS and the bucket). For a stricter first install, download `install.sh` and `install.sh.sig` and check the signature yourself with `keys/release.pub`.
* **Nothing runs without a plan.** Commands that change the system print a plan and need `--yes`.
* **Your files are yours.** BxRig keeps a config you changed and only rewrites files it wrote; every write is atomic, backed up and journaled.
* **Secrets** live in the desktop keyring (or a private file fallback), are typed hidden, and never appear in answers files, logs or shell history.
* **Skills** from the hub are audited; one that failed its audit is refused.

## Turn on a fingerprint or security key

`bxrig security` can turn on a fingerprint or a security key for `sudo`, the SSH server and passwordless sudo. These touch PAM and sudoers, so they are guarded.

```bash
bxrig security status
bxrig security fingerprint on --dry-run   # prints the exact PAM line first
bxrig security fingerprint on --yes
bxrig security fingerprint enroll --yes
bxrig security fido2 register --yes       # touch the key; `fido2 on` refuses until one is registered
bxrig security fido2 on --yes
bxrig security ssh-server on --yes
bxrig security passwordless-sudo on --yes
```

* **Only `/etc/pam.d/sudo` is changed** , never the login, the login screen or the lock screen. The line is `auth sufficient`, so your password still works when the reader or key is missing. The first time, the original is kept as `/etc/pam.d/sudo.bxrig-backup`; `off` removes exactly the line BxRig added.
* **sudoers** is checked with `visudo -cf` before the file is installed, so a mistake cannot lock sudo out.

> **Warning:** Passwordless sudo means any program running as you gets root without a password. Use it only on a machine where you accept that.
> **Note:** Keep a root terminal open the first time you try PAM changes. They have not been tried on a real reader or key yet.

## Advanced

### A GitHub source is not a release

`install.sh --source github:OWNER/REPO@REF` (for testing a branch) skips the signed release: there is no signature and no checksum from the BxRig downloads, so it warns and needs `--yes` or the typed word `unsigned`. Use it only for sources you trust. `GITHUB_TOKEN` or `GH_TOKEN` (private repositories) goes to GitHub as a header from a curl config on standard input, never on a command line, in the log or on screen.

### Where MatchBox comes from

The stable and snapshot builds are downloaded by `mvm` (an external installer script that the installer shows with its URL and SHA-256 before it runs). `--matchbox-branch REF` clones that branch of the repository you name and runs `cargo build` on it, which executes the repository's build scripts as your user: name only repositories you trust. The branch build is verified to run and recorded in `~/.local/share/bxrig/matchbox/build.info` (repo, branch, commit).

Next: [Updates and channels](/maintain/updates/index.html) · [MCP and privacy](/ai/mcp-and-privacy/index.html) · [Backups](/data/backups/index.html)

# Set up your dev machine

You will clone the repository, build `dist/bxrig`, and run the tests. The first run takes a while (it may build MatchBox); every run after that is quick.

## Quick start

1. Clone the repository.

   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/bxrig.git
   cd bxrig
   ```

2. Run the setup script once. It asks which MatchBox to use, builds `dist/bxrig`, runs a smoke test and sets up this machine.

   ```bash
   scripts/setup-local.sh
   ```

   To skip the question, name the choice:

   ```bash
   bash scripts/setup-local.sh --matchbox branch --matchbox-branch bxrig
   ```

3. Turn on the pre-commit hook so formatting never fails in CI.

   ```bash
   git config core.hooksPath .githooks
   ```

4. Check that everything works.

   ```bash
   dist/bxrig version
   tests/run-all.sh
   ```

> **Note:** Building needs a MatchBox with the terminal UI (`bif-tui`) and the class-file sharing fix. The script probes both and stops with the reason if one is missing. For now use the `branch` choice.

## The everyday loop

Each time you change code, do this.

```bash
scripts/dev-build.sh                 # rebuild dist/bxrig
dist/bxrig COMMAND --dry-run         # try your command by hand
tests/run-all.sh dist/bxrig NAME     # run the tests whose name contains NAME
bash scripts/format.sh               # tabs, LF, final newline
bash tests/dry-test.sh               # the ratchet and the CI test list
```

|          Script          |                                         What it does                                         |
|--------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `scripts/setup-local.sh` | Picks a MatchBox, saves it in `.cache/dev.env`, builds, smoke-tests, provisions the machine. |
| `scripts/dev-build.sh`   | Rebuilds `dist/bxrig` with the saved MatchBox. `MATCHBOX=/path/to/matchbox` overrides it.    |
| `scripts/format.sh`      | Formats the repository. `--check` lists what is unformatted and exits 1 (CI runs it first).  |
| `tests/run-all.sh`       | Runs every test. See [Tests](/developer/tests/index.html).                                   |
| `tests/dry-test.sh`      | The ratchet: banned patterns, the CI list and the format check.                              |

### Run from source, no build

The `.bxs` unit tests and one-off tries run straight from `src/`, so they need no build.

```bash
(cd src && matchbox ../tests/out_test.bxs)
```

`matchbox` is the one from `.cache/dev.env`, or the one on your `PATH`.

## Where things are

|                           Path                            |                                      Contents                                       |
|-----------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `src/Main.bx`                                             | The router: one `case` per command.                                                 |
| `src/bxrig/`                                              | One class per feature.                                                              |
| `src/bxrig/util/`                                         | Shared helpers: `Cli`, `Out`, `Exit`, `Mutation`, `Proc`, `Env`, `Text`, `Res`, ... |
| `docs/reference/cli.json`                                 | The command registry: summaries, usage, flags.                                      |
| `catalog/`, `templates/`, `themes/`, `skills/`, `assets/` | Data files packed into the binary.                                                  |
| `bootstrap/`                                              | The installer and the `gen-*.sh` scripts.                                           |
| `scripts/`                                                | Developer scripts (setup, build, format).                                           |
| `tests/`                                                  | `*-test.sh` with fake tools, `*_test.bxs` unit tests, `lib/` shared harness.        |
| `docs/`                                                   | This site. `docs/architecture/` holds the design records.                           |

## Advanced

### Choose another MatchBox

Name a branch, tag, fork or full commit id. Your own `../matchbox` checkout is never touched.

```bash
scripts/setup-local.sh --matchbox-branch develop
scripts/setup-local.sh --matchbox-branch feature/x --matchbox-repo someone/matchbox
scripts/setup-local.sh --matchbox-branch v0.14.0 --release
```

`BXRIG_MATCHBOX_BRANCH` and `BXRIG_MATCHBOX_REPO` do the same; the flags win. `stable` and `snapshot` come from `mvm`; the script stops if they fail the probes (the snapshot lacks the class-sharing fix for now).

### Build without touching the machine

After the build, `setup-local.sh` also installs packages and toolchains and starts `bxrig init`, like the web installer does.

|     Flag      |                            Effect                            |
|---------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|
| `--no-build`  | Only probe and save the choice.                              |
| `--no-setup`  | Build, but do not provision the machine.                     |
| `--no-wizard` | Provision, but skip `bxrig init`.                            |
| `--defaults`  | Run `bxrig init --defaults --yes` when there is no terminal. |

### Generated files

`Version.bx`, `WallpaperData.bx`, `CommandFlagData.bx`, `docs/reference/commands.md` and `command-flags.md` are generated. Change the source and run `bootstrap/gen-*.sh`; CI runs each with `--check`. `dev-build.sh` already runs `gen-assets.sh` and `gen-version.sh`.
