# The setup wizard

The wizard asks for your choices once, shows the commands it will run, and does nothing until you confirm. Re-run it any time with `bxrig init`.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Answer the pages"] --> B["Review: the exact commands"]
    B --> C{"Confirm?"}
    C -->|"yes"| D["Install screen"]
    C -->|"no"| E["Nothing changed"]
    D --> F["Summary and saved answers"]
```

`bxrig init` opens a full-screen form with these pages: **Desktop** , **Look** , **Top bar layout** , **App grid style** , **Theme** , **Input** , **Developer** , **Toolchains** , **Containers** , **NAS** , **Backups** (with the copy somewhere else), **Apps** , **AI** , **Extras** and **Import**, then a review screen that lists exactly the commands it will run. With the Customize choice on the Apps page there is one more page per catalog group. Nothing runs until you confirm.

|                                                                                                                                                |                                                                                                                                                         |
|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| ![The welcome screen](/assets/screenshots/wizard-welcome.webp) **Welcome**                                                                     | ![The Look page: dark or light, dock and bar position](/assets/screenshots/wizard-look.webp) **Look:** dark or light, dock, bar position                |
| ![The Look page: the world clock and its time zones](/assets/screenshots/wizard-world-clock.webp) **Look:** the world clock and its time zones | ![The Input page: keyboard layouts, scrolling, the Mac-style keys](/assets/screenshots/wizard-input.webp) **Input:** layouts, scrolling, shortcut style |

## The look pages

After **Look** (dark, light or auto, the dock, where the bar sits, the world clock) come three pages that show what you are choosing:

* **Top bar layout** (Hyprland and Both): Minimal, Standard (the default and the recommendation) or Dense. Each option draws its bar as a strip of text chips with the dock line below the list. Standard has the capture icon, Minimal does not, Dense adds brightness and weather. The arrow keys select as they move, so the strips and the description follow your cursor and Enter keeps what is highlighted. Later: `bxrig appearance bar layout minimal|standard|dense` or the Look page of the Control Center.
* **App grid style** (Hyprland and Both): Launchpad (the default, big colored tiles on a rounded card) or Terminal-style (flat glyphs, key hints, square corners). Both grids are drawn side by side and the arrow keys switch. Later: `bxrig appearance appgrid launchpad|terminal`.
* **Theme** (every desktop): every theme in `themes/` on a row with a swatch, `BxRig` the default. A pane next to the list shows the palette of the highlighted theme, read from its `colors.toml`, and a sample terminal in those colors. The wizard itself is drawn in the highlighted theme, so what you see is what the desktop will get. The icon set is not asked: BxRig's own icons are used. Later: `bxrig theme set NAME` or the Themes page of the Control Center.

On a terminal narrower than 92 columns (no step list) the Theme page keeps the list and the pane side by side; between 92 and 96 columns the pane is dropped and the rows keep their swatches.

The **Input** page asks about keyboard layouts, natural scrolling, and the shortcut style: "Mac-style Super keys" (on by default) and, when it is on, "Which keyboard do you type on?" (PC: Alt and Win are swapped so Alt acts as Cmd; Apple: no swap). When an Apple Magic or Logitech device is paired or plugged in (or the Mac-style keys are on) it also asks "Input devices" (default: detect); the answer becomes the optional step `bxrig input offer`, see [Mice, trackpads and keyboards](/desktop/input/index.html). Off keeps the Traditional keys (classic Super-key tiling keys). The answers become `bxrig keys style` and the xremap setup, which is installed either way because copy, paste, cut and select all are remaps in both styles. See [Shortcuts](/desktop/shortcuts/index.html).

## The install screen

When you press Enter on the review, the wizard stays on screen and installs. It does not drop back to a scrolling terminal.

* **Progress.** A bar in your theme's colours, `7 of 16 steps`, the step that runs now with a spinner and how long it has run, and the last line it printed. The apps step also shows its own count (`12 of 43`) while the package manager installs.
* **It says when it is quiet.** A download or a package build can print nothing for minutes. After 8 seconds without output the line says `no output for 42 s` and what the step is running right now (for example `pacman -S ...`, `makepkg`, `curl`), so a long step does not look stuck. Package installs, AUR builds and install scripts print as they go, so you see them in the log (`v`) while they run; a step that waits for a password shows as `sudo`.
* **`v` opens the log** under the bar: every line every step prints, live, with the step it came from. Arrows, PgUp and PgDn scroll it; `End` follows the newest line again; `v` closes it.
* **Ctrl+C asks first.** `y` stops: the running step is killed and the rest is not run.
* **When it ends** the screen shows what worked and what failed, with the exit code and the last line of each failure, and where the log and your answers are saved. `r` runs the failed steps again; Enter leaves. When the steps changed your session, groups or keys, `l` offers to log out (after a `y`); when they changed the boot screen, the login screen or a driver, `b` offers to reboot instead. Nothing happens without the `y`.
* **Your password once, on the screen.** The steps run in the background and the screen owns the terminal, so a sudo prompt could neither be seen nor answered. When sudo would ask for a password, the screen asks for it first (typed hidden, three tries, Esc cancels before anything runs). The steps then run with no terminal and a small helper that gives `sudo` the password. It lives in one file only you can read (mode 600, in a private folder under ``$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, which is memory, not disk), is never on a command line or in the log, and is deleted when the install ends. If you have no `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`` or no `setsid`, BxRig asks on the normal terminal before the screen starts instead, and relies on sudo's ticket. With a valid sudo ticket or `NOPASSWD`, nothing is asked.

A step that fails does not stop the others (a missing package should not cost you your keys and defaults): the plan goes on and the failure is shown at the end. Re-running the wizard repeats only what is still missing.

Some things are **skipped, not failed** , and the end says why and how to do them later: the LazyVim starter when `~/.config/nvim` already exists (your config is left alone), Podman's Docker compatibility when the `docker` package is installed (it conflicts with `podman-docker`: remove Docker first, or choose Docker as the engine), an app that conflicts with a package you have (timeshift next to CachyOS's `cachyos-snapper-support`), and an app your distribution's catalog does not offer. `bxrig init --dry-run` prints the first two as notes before anything runs.

### What it says when it ends

After you leave the screen the terminal keeps a summary:

    Done: 29 steps

    Already in place (nothing to do):
      editor-lazyvim  /home/you/.config/nvim already exists, so it was left alone. ...
                      later: bxrig editor lazyvim --yes
    Needs your decision:
      docker-compat   the docker package is installed and conflicts with podman-docker. ...
                      later: bxrig containers docker-compat --yes
    Skipped:
      session         SDDM's state folder /var/lib/sddm/ does not exist, so SDDM is not your login manager here. ...

    Saved:
      Your answers  ~/.config/bxrig/answers.json   (run them again: bxrig reinstall)
      The log       ~/.local/state/bxrig/logs/init-20261127-160037.log

    Next:
      1. Log out and back in, and pick Hyprland at the login screen: ... Log out now with: bxrig system logout --yes
      2. Open a new terminal to get the new shell and prompt.
      3. See what is set up on this machine: bxrig status        Change anything later: bxrig menu

Something that is already there (Boxy, a Neovim config of yours) is **in place** , not an error. A conflict (the `docker` package against Podman's Docker compatibility) **needs your decision** . Anything else that could not run here is **skipped** , each with the command to do it later. Your answers are saved in `~/.config/bxrig/answers.json`; run them again with `bxrig reinstall`, or change them and import the file with `bxrig init --from=FILE`.

### The log file

Every install writes a log you can read later or send for debugging: `~/.local/state/bxrig/logs/init-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.log`. It has the BxRig version and the system, the plan, each step's command, every line it printed, its exit code and how long it took, and every exception with its message and stack. Next to it, a folder of the same name holds each step's raw output. The last 20 runs are kept. The path is printed when the install ends and shown on the screen.

`bxrig init --plain` keeps the old streaming output instead of the screen, and `bxrig init --answers=FILE --yes --screen` runs a saved answers file on the screen. Both write the same log.

## How do you want to start?

After the welcome screen the wizard asks how to begin:

|             Choice             |                                                                                                                                                                                                                        What happens                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|--------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **New install**                | The whole wizard, page by page, from the defaults (what this machine already has is still marked `✓ installed`).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Import answers from a file** | You type the path of an answers file (`bxrig init --export=FILE` makes one; `~/` works). The answers go on top of the defaults and you land on the **review**, ready to go. Esc on the review goes back to the pages if you want to change something. A file that is not there, or is not an answers file, is an error on the screen; keys this version does not ask are ignored and counted ("Imported 24 answers from ... (2 not used by this version)"). |
| **Use my saved answers**       | Shown only when you have run the wizard before: your last answers plus what the machine has, straight to the review.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

`bxrig init --fresh`, `--rerun` and `--from=FILE` already say how to begin, so they skip this question.

## Run it again

On a machine that is already set up the wizard starts from your saved answers plus what it finds on the system, and marks installed options with `✓ installed`.

|         Command          |                    Starts from                    |
|--------------------------|---------------------------------------------------|
| `bxrig init`             | your saved answers and what the system has (tune) |
| `bxrig init --rerun`     | your saved answers only                           |
| `bxrig init --fresh`     | the defaults                                      |
| `bxrig init --from=FILE` | an answers file from another machine              |

Nothing the machine already has is ever removed. `bxrig status` shows the same scan without opening the wizard.

## Without a terminal

```bash
bxrig init --answers=answers.json --yes     # apply an answers file
bxrig init --defaults --yes                  # the wizard's default answers
bxrig init --dry-run                         # show the plan only
bxrig init --export=answers.json             # save your answers for another machine
```

Answers are saved in `~/.config/bxrig/answers.json` (mode 600). They never contain secrets.

## Defaults worth knowing

|        Question        |                           Default                           |
|------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|
| Desktop                | Hyprland + Noctalia                                         |
| Shortcut style         | Mac-style Super keys on a PC keyboard (Alt and Win swapped) |
| Top bar layout         | Standard                                                    |
| App grid style         | Launchpad                                                   |
| Color theme            | BxRig                                                       |
| Default browser        | Brave                                                       |
| Launcher, menu program | Vicinae, Vicinae                                            |
| Workspaces             | 4                                                           |
| Shell                  | zsh with the Starship prompt (Catppuccin Powerline)         |
| Terminal               | Ghostty                                                     |
| File manager           | Strata                                                      |
| Toolchains             | Java and Rust                                               |
| Containers             | Podman (with `docker` commands mapped to it)                |
| Dictation              | Superwhisper (Voxtype is the alternative)                   |
| Updates                | stable channel, daily notification                          |

## What is always installed

BoxLang, Java 21 (switched with jenv) and Rust (rustup, stable) are part of the stack, so the Toolchains page does not ask about them. It asks for extra Java versions (21 stays global), the IDEs and editors you want (VS Code, IntelliJ IDEA Community, Zed, Cursor, Sublime Text) and the other toolchains. The BoxLang extension question only appears when VS Code is ticked.

## When things are installed

The review lists the steps in order. Apps, including the IDEs and any local model apps you ticked, come first. The local AI setup (llama.cpp and the model downloads) is one step near the end, and only runs when you answered "now"; otherwise nothing is downloaded.

## When it finishes

The last screen is a summary: what failed (press `r` to retry), what to do next (log out, reboot, open a new terminal), what needs your decision, what was skipped and the command to do it later, and where your answers and log are saved. Press `d` to see every step.

# Your NAS

Use this page to connect a Synology or any SMB or NFS share, mount it automatically and use it as a place for backups. `bxrig nas` keeps every NAS you use: its address, the share, how to reach it, and the mount.

## Try it

```bash
bxrig nas setup --yes                   # cifs-utils, nfs-utils, smbclient, avahi, rsync
bxrig nas discover                      # find NAS boxes on the network
bxrig nas add synology --host=ds920.local --user=luis --ask-password
bxrig nas mount synology backups --yes  # ~/NAS/synology/backups
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["nas discover"] --> B["nas add"]
  B --> C["nas shares"]
  C --> D["nas mount"]
  D --> E["nas auto on"]
  D --> F["nas use: a backup place"]
  D --> G["nas sync: rsync mirror"]
```

The diagram shows the path from finding a NAS to using it for mounts, backups and copies.

## Connect and mount

```bash
bxrig nas shares synology
bxrig nas mount synology backups --yes  # ~/NAS/synology/backups
bxrig nas auto on synology backups --yes
bxrig nas test synology
```

* **`nas auto on`** makes systemd `.mount` and `.automount` units: the share mounts the first time something opens it and lets go after ten idle minutes, so a sleeping NAS never blocks your login.
* **`nas test`** checks that the NAS answers, that your password works, that the share is mounted and writable, and how much space is free.

## Back up to it

```bash
bxrig nas use synology backups          # a place for bxrig backup data
```

Then continue with [Backups](/data/backups/index.html).

## Copy files to it

`nas sync NAME SRC --to=SHARE/PATH` is a plain `rsync` mirror (photos, media). Nothing on the NAS is deleted unless you add `--delete`.

## Advanced

* **Passwords** are typed hidden and kept in your keyring. SMB mounts are made by root (also at boot), so the password is also kept in `/etc/bxrig/nas/NAME.cred`, readable by root only; the plan tells you before it writes it. NFS needs no password.
* **The SMB version** is negotiated: the highest one the NAS and your kernel both support. Give `--vers=3.1.1` to choose.

> **Note:** Not yet tried on a real Synology: share permissions in DSM, SMB signing and NFS export options. If a mount fails, `bxrig nas test NAME` says which step.

Next: [Backups](/data/backups/index.html) · [Scheduler](/data/scheduler/index.html)

title: Add a theme
body: Add a theme You will add a new bundled theme called sunset . One folder with a colors.toml is enough to make it appear in bxrig theme list , the Themes page and the theme switcher. Files you touch File What for themes/sunset/colors.toml The palette (required). themes/sunset/neovim.lua The Neovim colorscheme plugin spec (optional but expected). assets/wallpapers/sunset.jpg The wallpaper, 2560x1440 JPEG (optional). src/bxrig/WallpaperData.bx Generated: the wallpaper names and SHA-256. Never edit by hand. tests/theme-test.sh The theme counts the test checks. docs/customize/themes.md The theme table and the count. What happens to your file This diagram shows how one colors.toml becomes the files each tool reads. flowchart LR A["themes/NAME/colors.toml"] --> B["ThemeColors parse"] B --> C["Noctalia palette"] B --> D["Terminals: ghostty kitty alacritty foot"] B --> E["btop, tmux, fzf, rofi, fuzzel, wofi"] B --> F["GTK, Qt, Plasma colors"] B --> G["Hyprland accent"] H["neovim.lua"] --> I["Neovim colorscheme"] J["NAME.jpg"] --> K["Wallpaper"] bxrig theme set NAME writes these files through the config service (atomic, backed up) and then tells the running desktop. Steps Copy a theme that is close to what you want. cp -r themes/nord themes/sunset Edit themes/sunset/colors.toml . Every color is #rrggbb . mode = "dark" accent = "#ff7a59" selection = "#4a2f3a" muted = "#7a5f6a" background = "#2a1b24" dark_background = "#201219" darker_background = "#180d13" lighter_background = "#38242f" foreground = "#f3e3dc" dark_foreground = "#8a7078" light_foreground = "#d9c3bb" bright_foreground = "#fff1ea" red = "#e5566d" yellow = "#f0c36d" orange = "#f08a5d" green = "#9ccc8a" cyan = "#7fcfd0" blue = "#6f9bd8" magenta = "#c78ad0" brown = "#6a4b3d" bright_red = "#f0788a" bright_yellow = "#f7d58f" bright_green = "#b4dca4" bright_cyan = "#a0e0e0" bright_blue = "#8fb4e8" bright_magenta = "#d9a6e0" Only accent , background , foreground , red , green , yellow , blue , magenta and cyan are required. A missing one, or a value that is not #rrggbb , rejects the whole theme (it is never half applied). mode is "dark" or "light" . Optional: name a font. The id comes from bxrig appearance font list . Once that font is installed, theme set makes it the shell and terminal font. font = "sharetech" Add themes/sunset/neovim.lua : a LazyVim plugin spec that installs a colorscheme and selects it. Copy the one from the theme you started from and change the plugin and the colorscheme name. # Add a theme

You will add a new bundled theme called `sunset`. One folder with a `colors.toml` is enough to make it appear in `bxrig theme list`, the Themes page and the theme switcher.

## Files you touch

|              File              |                            What for                             |
|--------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------|
| `themes/sunset/colors.toml`    | The palette (required).                                         |
| `themes/sunset/neovim.lua`     | The Neovim colorscheme plugin spec (optional but expected).     |
| `assets/wallpapers/sunset.jpg` | The wallpaper, 2560x1440 JPEG (optional).                       |
| `src/bxrig/WallpaperData.bx`   | Generated: the wallpaper names and SHA-256. Never edit by hand. |
| `tests/theme-test.sh`          | The theme counts the test checks.                               |
| `docs/customize/themes.md`     | The theme table and the count.                                  |

## What happens to your file

This diagram shows how one `colors.toml` becomes the files each tool reads.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["themes/NAME/colors.toml"] --> B["ThemeColors parse"]
  B --> C["Noctalia palette"]
  B --> D["Terminals: ghostty kitty alacritty foot"]
  B --> E["btop, tmux, fzf, rofi, fuzzel, wofi"]
  B --> F["GTK, Qt, Plasma colors"]
  B --> G["Hyprland accent"]
  H["neovim.lua"] --> I["Neovim colorscheme"]
  J["NAME.jpg"] --> K["Wallpaper"]
```

`bxrig theme set NAME` writes these files through the config service (atomic, backed up) and then tells the running desktop.

## Steps

1. Copy a theme that is close to what you want.

   ```bash
   cp -r themes/nord themes/sunset
   ```

2. Edit `themes/sunset/colors.toml`. Every color is `#rrggbb`.

   ```toml
   mode = "dark"

   accent = "#ff7a59"
   selection = "#4a2f3a"
   muted = "#7a5f6a"

   background = "#2a1b24"
   dark_background = "#201219"
   darker_background = "#180d13"
   lighter_background = "#38242f"

   foreground = "#f3e3dc"
   dark_foreground = "#8a7078"
   light_foreground = "#d9c3bb"
   bright_foreground = "#fff1ea"

   red = "#e5566d"
   yellow = "#f0c36d"
   orange = "#f08a5d"
   green = "#9ccc8a"
   cyan = "#7fcfd0"
   blue = "#6f9bd8"
   magenta = "#c78ad0"
   brown = "#6a4b3d"

   bright_red = "#f0788a"
   bright_yellow = "#f7d58f"
   bright_green = "#b4dca4"
   bright_cyan = "#a0e0e0"
   bright_blue = "#8fb4e8"
   bright_magenta = "#d9a6e0"
   ```

   Only `accent`, `background`, `foreground`, `red`, `green`, `yellow`, `blue`, `magenta` and `cyan` are required. A missing one, or a value that is not `#rrggbb`, rejects the whole theme (it is never half applied). `mode` is `"dark"` or `"light"`.
3. Optional: name a font. The id comes from `bxrig appearance font list`. Once that font is installed, `theme set` makes it the shell and terminal font.

   ```toml
   font = "sharetech"
   ```

4. Add `themes/sunset/neovim.lua`: a LazyVim plugin spec that installs a colorscheme and selects it. Copy the one from the theme you started from and change the plugin and the `colorscheme` name.

5. Optional: add a wallpaper as `assets/wallpapers/sunset.jpg` (2560x1440), then regenerate the hashes.

   ```bash
   bootstrap/gen-assets.sh
   ```

   Wallpapers are not packed into the binary. `bxrig.Wallpapers` finds a copy, checks its SHA-256 and copies it to `~/Pictures/BxRig/sunset.jpg`, or downloads it from the release site when missing. A theme without a wallpaper leaves the user's own.
6. Update `tests/theme-test.sh`: the theme count (`length == 24`, twice in the `list` check) goes up by one, and a light theme must be added to the list of light names. The `22` generated files per theme do not change.

## See it working

```bash
scripts/dev-build.sh
dist/bxrig theme list              # sunset appears, valid
dist/bxrig theme show sunset
dist/bxrig theme set sunset --dry-run
dist/bxrig tui themes              # the swatch, preview and wallpaper
```

The theme list, the Themes page and the theme switcher all read the same list, so there is nothing to register.

## Test it

```bash
tests/theme-test.sh dist/bxrig
```

The test sets themes against fake desktop tools and checks the generated files. Also see `tests/theme_colors_test.bxs` for the color maths.

## Document it

In `docs/customize/themes.md` update the count, the list of names and the gallery table. If you have a desktop, capture a screenshot with the wallpaper and `btop` in a themed terminal.
> **Screenshot wanted:** the new theme applied, wallpaper plus `btop` in a themed terminal, saved as `docs/assets/screenshots/themes/sunset.webp`.

## Common mistakes

* A color without the leading `#`, or in short `#abc` form: the theme is rejected as invalid.
* Forgetting `bootstrap/gen-assets.sh` after adding a wallpaper: the SHA-256 is unknown and the wallpaper is never used.
* Editing a generated file by hand: `theme set` rewrites them all on every change.
* A name with capitals or spaces: names are lower case letters, digits and dashes. Names that start with `bxrig` count as BxRig's own, the rest as community themes (credit them in `themes/NOTICE.md`).

## Advanced

* Two `colors.toml` shapes are read: the named one above, and the older one with `color0` to `color15`, `cursor` and `selection_*`. In the named shape the terminal palette comes from the roles: black is `background`, white is `foreground`, bright black is `muted`, bright white is `bright_foreground`.
* Where a theme is found, first match wins: `~/.config/bxrig/themes`, then Omarchy folders, then the bundled ones. A user folder with the same name beats yours.
* Users can add themes without a rebuild: `bxrig theme import DIR --name=NAME`.
* Next: [Add a command](/developer/add-a-command/index.html), [Tests](/developer/tests/index.html).

# Boxy's look and voice

Give Boxy, the desktop assistant `bxrig ai agents setup` makes, a name, a colour and outfits, and talk to it by holding a key. **Nothing here is on until you turn it on:** no microphone, no speech, no outfit other than the season's.

## Try it

```bash
bxrig boxy                                     # Boxy now, as text
bxrig boxy look --name=Pixel --color='#ff8800' # a name and a colour (the default follows your theme)
bxrig boxy look --holidays=christmas,halloween --birthday=03-09
bxrig boxy export                              # the four pictures
```

![Boxy's four states](/assets/screenshots/boxy-states.webp)

## Look

* **Colour** follows your theme's accent unless you pick one with `--color`.
* **Outfits** follow the season in `auto`: a beanie in winter, a flower in spring, sunglasses in summer, a leaf in autumn. Holiday outfits (`christmas`, `halloween`, `newyear`) appear only for the holidays you list, and the party hat on your birthday. `--outfit=none` turns it all off, or pick one: `beanie`, `flower`, `sunglasses`, `leaf`, `santa`, `pumpkin`, `party`.
* **Four pictures:** Boxy is an antenna bot. The tip of its antenna is the BoxLang swirl: it is lit and turns while Boxy works, the antenna leans while it listens, and the mouth opens when it speaks. The bar shows the one for what Boxy is doing; `bxrig boxy export` writes them as PNG (SVG without `rsvg-convert` or ImageMagick). The working swirl has four pictures, so it turns.
* **In a terminal** it is a small text sprite, like `[ •‿• ]`, with the outfit as a hat above.

## Your conversations and logs

BxRig keeps no copy of your chats. They are bx-agents' own (`~/.bxagents/Boxy/chat.db`), and you open them there:

* **Chat in a terminal:** `bxrig ai agents chat`, Super+Period, or the bar's Boxy tab, **Chat**. It joins the running Boxy, so your earlier chats are there.
* **The web page:** `bxrig ai agents open`, Super+Shift+Period, or **Web** in the bar tab: chats, files and skills.
* **Logs:** `bxrig ai agents Boxy logs --ui` (a full-screen viewer), or **Logs** in the bar tab.

What you say with the hold-to-talk key goes into the same Boxy, as the conversation `bxrig-voice`.

![The Boxy tab in the bar](/assets/screenshots/boxy-bar.webp)

The Control Center has a Boxy page (`bxrig tui boxy`): Enter on an outfit puts it on.

![The Boxy page](/assets/screenshots/boxy-page.webp)

## Talk to it

Install Voxtype (`bxrig dictation setup voxtype`), then **hold Super+Comma, speak, let go**. The Copilot key (Super+Shift+F23) does the same. In the Mac key style the key is Super+Ctrl+Slash, since Super+Comma is Preferences there. The bar's Boxy tab has a Talk button as well.

Your words go to Boxy like a typed question. The answer comes as a notice. **If Boxy wants to change something, it waits for you on screen: approving is never done by voice.**

## Let it speak

Speech is off. Turn it on with a voice that runs on this machine (`bxrig boxy voice local --yes`) or with a server (`bxrig boxy voice set`). The details are under Advanced.

## Advanced

### Speech setup

There are two ways to turn speech on.

#### On this machine, in English and Spanish

Boxy can speak with [bx-audio](https://github.com/ortus-boxlang/bx-audio), a BoxLang module that runs the voices on your own machine. Nothing Boxy says leaves it.

```bash
install-bx-module bx-audio
bxrig boxy voice local                     # the plan: voices, accent, download size
bxrig boxy voice local --yes               # English and Spanish, Latin American accent
bxrig boxy voice test --lang=es
```

The first `--yes` downloads the speech engine and the voices (about 350 MB, once). Then:

|           Option            |                                                                                                   What it does                                                                                                    |
|-----------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `--lang=auto\|en\|es`       | `auto` (the default) speaks each answer in the language it is written in. `en` or `es` always uses that language                                                                                                  |
| `--voice=NAME`              | the voice for the language you name with `--lang=en` or `--lang=es`. `bxrig boxy voice list --lang=es` shows the choices (`dora`, `alex`, `santa_es`)                                                             |
| `--accent=latam\|castilian` | how Spanish sounds: Latin American (the default, `z` and `ce`, `ci` as `s`) or Castilian (as `th`)                                                                                                                |
| `--speed=N`                 | 1 is the voice's own pace, 1.2 faster, 0.85 slower                                                                                                                                                                |
| `--hear=auto\|en\|es`       | the language Voxtype listens for when you hold the key. Sets `language` in `[whisper]` of `~/.config/voxtype/config.toml`. For Spanish use a multilingual Voxtype model (not an `.en` one): `voxtype setup model` |

Boxy tells the language by its letters and its small words (`el`, `de`, `que`, `the`, `and`). Short or mixed text can be wrong: set `--lang=en` or `--lang=es` if you always use one.

#### With a server

Point it at any OpenAI-compatible `/v1/audio/speech` server:

```bash
bxrig secrets set OPENAI_API_KEY
bxrig boxy voice set --url=https://api.openai.com/v1/audio/speech --model=tts-1 --voice=alloy --key=OPENAI_API_KEY
bxrig boxy voice on
bxrig boxy say "hello"
```

With a cloud server, each answer Boxy reads aloud is sent there: `bxrig boxy voice` and `bxrig privacy` both say where. A speech server on this machine works the same way, with a `127.0.0.1` URL. Either way it needs one of `pw-play`, `paplay`, `ffplay` or `mpv`. `bxrig boxy voice set` goes back to a server; `bxrig boxy voice local --yes` goes back to bx-audio.

### Not tested on real hardware

The commands and the keys are tested with fake tools. The first real run (your microphone, Voxtype's service, the key release, and the picture in the bar) is on your machine.

Next: [Appearance](/customize/appearance/index.html), [BoxLang agents](/ai/boxlang-agents/index.html).

markdown:
# Mail catcher

When you build an app that sends email, you want to see the mail without sending it to anyone. `bxrig mail` runs a catcher in a container ([Mailpit](https://mailpit.axllent.org)): your app sends to `127.0.0.1:1025` and the mail shows up in an inbox. Nothing leaves your machine.

## Try it

```bash
bxrig mail start --yes        # plan first without --yes
bxrig mail test               # send one sample message
bxrig mail open               # the web inbox in your browser
```

It needs a container engine: Podman by default, or Docker (`bxrig db engine docker`).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["Your app"] -->|"SMTP 1025"| B["Mailpit container"]
  B --> C["Web inbox 8025"]
  B --> D["bxrig mail list"]
  B --> E["Control Center Mail page"]
```

The diagram shows where your app's mail goes.

## Point your app at it

`bxrig mail env` prints the settings for BoxLang and ColdBox apps, Laravel, Spring Boot, Node and plain environment variables. In short: host `127.0.0.1`, port `1025`, no encryption, no username or password.

## Read the mail

```bash
bxrig mail list               # what arrived
bxrig mail show ID            # headers, text body and attachments
bxrig mail clear --yes        # delete every message
bxrig mail stop
```

`bxrig tui` has a Mail page. It lists the messages (newest first), shows the headers and text of the highlighted one, and refreshes itself every few seconds so you can watch mail arrive. `d` deletes a message, `c` clears the inbox, `o` opens it rendered in your browser and `t` sends a test message. Deleting and clearing show a plan first.

The setup wizard has a yes or no question for the mail catcher (off by default). The task menu has Develop \> Mail catcher.

## Keep the mail between runs

Without `--keep`, stopping the catcher deletes it and its mail. That is what you want while developing: every run starts with an empty inbox. If you want the mail to survive, start it with `bxrig mail start --keep --yes`; it is then stored in `~/.local/share/bxrig/mail`. `bxrig mail remove --yes` deletes the container and any stored mail (`--keep-data` keeps the folder).

## Advanced

The catcher listens on `127.0.0.1` only: SMTP on port 1025 (no TLS, any login is accepted) and the web inbox on port 8025. Change the ports with `--smtp-port=2525` and `--ui-port=9025`.

Next: [Databases and virtual machines](/build/databases-and-vms/index.html) · [Developer tools](/build/developer-tools/index.html)

title: MCP and privacy
body: MCP and privacy Use this page to give your coding agent BxRig's tools, and to see and limit what your AI tools send out. Try it bxrig mcp link --yes # BxRig's tools in every agent you have, read-only bxrig privacy # what leaves this machine bxrig privacy local-only --yes # use your local model where an agent can Give your agent BxRig's tools Your coding agent or editor can use BxRig the way Boxy does: ask how the battery is, list the themes, check your agenda, search the app catalog, see your databases. BxRig gives them its tools over MCP (Model Context Protocol), which every major agent speaks. flowchart LR A["Your agent or editor"] -->|"MCP"| B["bxrig mcp serve"] B --> C["BxRig command"] C --> D{"Read or change?"} D -->|"read"| E["Runs"] D -->|"change (needs --write)"| F["Agent asks you first"] The diagram shows how an agent's request reaches BxRig and where the read-only limit applies. bxrig mcp # each agent and editor: linked or not bxrig mcp link --yes # every one you have installed, read-only bxrig mcp link pi-agent --write --yes # one agent, and it may change things too bxrig mcp tools # the tools: what reads and what changes bxrig mcp unlink --yes Read-only unless you say so. A linked agent gets 17 tools that only read. With --write it also gets the 19 that change something (the theme, night light, reminders, installing an app, starting a database, a system update) and, like for its own tools, it asks you before each one. The same tools as Boxy. They are Boxy's own tools, so each one runs a BxRig command: an agent can do only what BxRig does, through the same plans and checks. What it runs on. The server is BoxLang with bx-ai, which bx-agents installs: bxrig ai agents install --yes once. The agent starts bxrig mcp serve itself, for its session. See what leaves your machine bxrig privacy For each AI on this machine: where its model runs (here or in the cloud, and whose), whether it could use your local model, the keys you stored (by name, never a value), the MCP servers each agent can reach and where they are, each agent's telemetry, and the folders where agents keep your chats. The Privacy page ( bxrig tui privacy ) shows the same report as rows: a cloud agent that could be local and a web MCP server are flagged. l turns local-only on ( L off), t turns telemetry off ( T back on). The bar's Agents panel has a Privacy button that opens it. Use your local model The agents that can use a local model get BxRig's server, 127.0.0.1:8089 (see Local AI ): bxrig privacy local-only --yes # OpenCode, Pi, Copilot CLI, Crush, Goose bxrig privacy local-only --off --yes OpenCode also makes your active model its default; in the others pick the BxRig provider. Turn off telemetry Where the agent has a documented switch: bxrig privacy telemetry off --yes bxrig privacy telemetry on zed --yes # one agent back to its own default Advanced Which agents can go local The rest can not use a local model, and the report says why: Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Antigravity and Kiro only offer their makers' models, and Cursor and Amp send every request through their own servers. Kilo Code, Qwen Code, Grok Build, Zed, VS Code and Codex can be pointed at it by hand; the report says where (Codex needs the Responses API, which only recent llama.cpp builds offer). What the telemetry switch sets Agent What BxRig sets Claude Code DISABLE_TELEMETRY and DISABLE_ERROR_REPORTING in ~/.claude/settings.json Codex [analytics] enabled = false Gemini CLI, Qwen Code privacy.usageStatisticsEnabled: false Pi enableInstallTelemetry: false Goose GOOSE_TELEMETRY_ENABLED: false Kiro kiro-cli settings telemetry.enabled false Zed telemetry.diagnostics and telemetry.metrics off VS Code telemetry.telemetryLevel: off For the others the report says how, when there is a way: Crush with CRUSH_DISABLE_METRICS=1 in your shell, Cursor with Privacy Mode in your account, Antigravity in its settings. Kilo Code has one you set yourself: KILO_TELEMETRY_LEVEL=off in your environment. OpenCode, Amp and Grok Build document no switch. # MCP and privacy

Use this page to give your coding agent BxRig's tools, and to see and limit what your AI tools send out.

## Try it

```bash
bxrig mcp link --yes              # BxRig's tools in every agent you have, read-only
bxrig privacy                     # what leaves this machine
bxrig privacy local-only --yes    # use your local model where an agent can
```

## Give your agent BxRig's tools

Your coding agent or editor can use BxRig the way Boxy does: ask how the battery is, list the themes, check your agenda, search the app catalog, see your databases. BxRig gives them its tools over MCP (Model Context Protocol), which every major agent speaks.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["Your agent or editor"] -->|"MCP"| B["bxrig mcp serve"]
  B --> C["BxRig command"]
  C --> D{"Read or change?"}
  D -->|"read"| E["Runs"]
  D -->|"change (needs --write)"| F["Agent asks you first"]
```

The diagram shows how an agent's request reaches BxRig and where the read-only limit applies.

```bash
bxrig mcp                         # each agent and editor: linked or not
bxrig mcp link --yes              # every one you have installed, read-only
bxrig mcp link pi-agent --write --yes   # one agent, and it may change things too
bxrig mcp tools                   # the tools: what reads and what changes
bxrig mcp unlink --yes
```

**Read-only unless you say so.** A linked agent gets 17 tools that only read. With `--write` it also gets the 19 that change something (the theme, night light, reminders, installing an app, starting a database, a system update) and, like for its own tools, it asks you before each one.

**The same tools as Boxy.** They are Boxy's own tools, so each one runs a BxRig command: an agent can do only what BxRig does, through the same plans and checks.

**What it runs on.** The server is BoxLang with bx-ai, which [bx-agents](/ai/boxlang-agents/index.html) installs: `bxrig ai agents install --yes` once. The agent starts `bxrig mcp serve` itself, for its session.

## See what leaves your machine

```bash
bxrig privacy
```

![What leaves this machine](/assets/screenshots/privacy-cli.webp)

For each AI on this machine: where its model runs (here or in the cloud, and whose), whether it could use your local model, the keys you stored (by name, never a value), the MCP servers each agent can reach and where they are, each agent's telemetry, and the folders where agents keep your chats.

The **Privacy** page (`bxrig tui privacy`) shows the same report as rows: a cloud agent that could be local and a web MCP server are flagged. `l` turns local-only on (`L` off), `t` turns telemetry off (`T` back on). The bar's Agents panel has a **Privacy** button that opens it.

![The Privacy page of the Control Center](/assets/screenshots/privacy-page.webp)

## Use your local model

The agents that can use a local model get BxRig's server, `127.0.0.1:8089` (see [Local AI](/ai/local-ai/index.html)):

```bash
bxrig privacy local-only --yes        # OpenCode, Pi, Copilot CLI, Crush, Goose
bxrig privacy local-only --off --yes
```

OpenCode also makes your active model its default; in the others pick the BxRig provider.

## Turn off telemetry

Where the agent has a documented switch:

```bash
bxrig privacy telemetry off --yes
bxrig privacy telemetry on zed --yes   # one agent back to its own default
```

## Advanced

### Which agents can go local

The rest can not use a local model, and the report says why: Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Antigravity and Kiro only offer their makers' models, and Cursor and Amp send every request through their own servers. Kilo Code, Qwen Code, Grok Build, Zed, VS Code and Codex can be pointed at it by hand; the report says where (Codex needs the Responses API, which only recent llama.cpp builds offer).

### What the telemetry switch sets

|         Agent         |                                What BxRig sets                                 |
|-----------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Claude Code           | `DISABLE_TELEMETRY` and `DISABLE_ERROR_REPORTING` in `~/.claude/settings.json` |
| Codex                 | `[analytics] enabled = false`                                                  |
| Gemini CLI, Qwen Code | `privacy.usageStatisticsEnabled: false`                                        |
| Pi                    | `enableInstallTelemetry: false`                                                |
| Goose                 | `GOOSE_TELEMETRY_ENABLED: false`                                               |
| Kiro                  | `kiro-cli settings telemetry.enabled false`                                    |
| Zed                   | `telemetry.diagnostics` and `telemetry.metrics` off                            |
| VS Code               | `telemetry.telemetryLevel: off`                                                |

For the others the report says how, when there is a way: Crush with `CRUSH_DISABLE_METRICS=1` in your shell, Cursor with Privacy Mode in your account, Antigravity in its settings. Kilo Code has one you set yourself: `KILO_TELEMETRY_LEVEL=off` in your environment. OpenCode, Amp and Grok Build document no switch.

### Where `mcp link` writes

`link` writes only BxRig's own entry, in each agent's own place, and keeps the old file as `FILE.bxrig-backup`:

|     Agent or editor     |                              Where                              |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------|
| Claude Code, Codex      | their own `mcp add` command                                     |
| Pi                      | `~/.pi/agent/mcp.json`                                          |
| Gemini CLI              | `~/.gemini/settings.json`                                       |
| OpenCode                | `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`                              |
| Kilo Code               | `~/.config/kilo/kilo.json` (or `kilo.jsonc` when you have that) |
| GitHub Copilot CLI      | `~/.copilot/mcp-config.json`                                    |
| Cursor and Cursor Agent | `~/.cursor/mcp.json`                                            |
| Amp                     | `~/.config/amp/settings.json`                                   |
| Crush                   | `~/.config/crush/crushrc`                                       |
| Goose                   | `~/.config/goose/config.yaml`                                   |
| Kiro                    | `~/.kiro/settings/mcp.json`                                     |
| Qwen Code               | `~/.qwen/settings.json`                                         |
| Grok Build              | `~/.grok/config.toml`                                           |
| Antigravity             | `~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json`                              |
| Zed                     | `~/.config/zed/settings.json` (your comments stay)              |
| VS Code                 | `~/.config/Code/User/mcp.json`                                  |

A file BxRig can not change safely (JSON with comments where the agent does not allow them, or an entry of yours in the way) is left out with the reason; name the agent to see it as an error. Restart an agent that is running to see the tools.

Next: [AI agents and skills](/ai/agents/index.html) · [Local AI](/ai/local-ai/index.html) · [Security](/maintain/security/index.html)

# Scheduler

Use this page to see what runs on a timer and to add your own tasks. BxRig runs its timed work on one scheduler: a BoxLang scheduler class on the BoxLang JVM, kept running by a user service. It runs the daily update check, your file backups, the BoxLang and module checks, and any task you add. Every run is recorded, so you can see what ran, how long it took and what failed.

## Try it

```bash
bxrig scheduler install --yes        # once: the service, the built-in tasks, and the old timers turned off
bxrig scheduler                      # every task: group, schedule, next run, how the last run went
bxrig scheduler run backup-data      # run it now (recorded like a scheduled run)
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["schedule.json"] --> B["Scheduler.bx runner"]
  B --> C["bxrig-scheduler.service"]
  C -->|"on time"| D["bxrig scheduler exec NAME"]
  D --> E["Your command"]
  D --> F["History and stats"]
  D --> G["Notice if it failed"]
```

The diagram shows how a task goes from the list to a recorded run.

## Look at a task

```bash
bxrig scheduler show backup-data     # its command, stats (runs, failures, success rate, average time) and recent runs
```

## Use the task manager

`bxrig tui tasks` (or Control Center \> Tasks, or System \> Scheduler \> Task manager in the menu) lists every task with how its last run went, when it runs next and a sparkline of its recent runs.

| Mark |                     Means                      |
|------|------------------------------------------------|
| ✓    | the last run went well                         |
| !    | it needs your attention (an update is waiting) |
| ✗    | it failed or timed out                         |
| ·    | it has not run yet                             |
| ‖    | paused                                         |

`Enter` shows the task: its command, runs, failures, success rate, average time, the trend of its last 30 runs, recent runs and the last output. `r` runs it now, `p` pauses or resumes it, `g` pauses or resumes its group, `a` adds a task (name, when, command), `x` removes one of yours (the built-in ones can be paused, not removed).

The **System panel** has a Tasks tab: whether the scheduler runs (with Install when it does not), a card for each failing task with its last output, Run again, Show and Pause, and the next runs. While a task is failing, the System icon in the bar has a red dot.

`bxrig doctor --dev` has a scheduler row, and the setup wizard offers to install the scheduler.

## Add your own tasks

```bash
bxrig scheduler add photos-to-nas --when="daily 23:00" --group=sync -- rsync -a ~/Pictures/ nas:/photos/
bxrig scheduler add tidy-downloads --when="weekly sun 10:00" -- bxrig files tidy
bxrig scheduler pause sync           # every task in a group
bxrig scheduler resume sync
bxrig scheduler disable tidy-downloads
bxrig scheduler remove tidy-downloads
```

|              `--when`               |                     Runs                     |
|-------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------|
| `every 15 minutes`, `every 2 hours` | from the time the scheduler starts           |
| `hourly`                            | every hour                                   |
| `daily 02:30`                       | every day at 02:30                           |
| `weekdays 09:00`                    | Monday to Friday at 09:00                    |
| `weekly mon 09:00`                  | every Monday at 09:00                        |
| `cron 0 2 * * *`                    | a 5-field cron (needs BoxLang 1.20 or newer) |

A command after `--` that starts with `bxrig` runs with your BxRig; anything else runs as it is. `--notify` is `failure` (the default: a notice when a run fails or times out), `attention` (also when it exits 10, "something needs you"), `always` or `never`. `--timeout` is in seconds (one hour by default).

## See what it replaces

|           Before           |                                                Now                                                 |
|----------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `bxrig-update-check.timer` | the task `update-check` (daily, group `system`)                                                    |
| `bxrig-backup.timer`       | the task `backup-data` (hourly or daily 02:30, group `backups`)                                    |
| nothing                    | the task `boxlang-check` (daily, group `boxlang`): a notice when BoxLang or a module has an update |

Once the scheduler is installed, `bxrig update notifications on|off` and `bxrig backup data schedule hourly|daily|off` change those tasks instead of writing timers.

## Advanced

### How it works

* `~/.config/bxrig/schedule.json` holds the tasks. Change them with `bxrig scheduler`, not by hand.
* `~/.local/share/bxrig/scheduler/Scheduler.bx` is the runner, written by BxRig: one BoxLang scheduled task per enabled task. It is written again on every change and the service restarts.
* `bxrig-scheduler.service` runs `boxlang schedule` on it and restarts it if it stops.
* Each run calls `bxrig scheduler exec NAME`, which runs the command, adds a line to `~/.local/state/bxrig/scheduler/history/NAME.jsonl` (the last 500 runs) and sends the notice. After each run the runner writes the task's BoxLang `getStats()` (next run, last run, totals) to `stats/NAME.json`.

`bxrig scheduler uninstall --yes` stops the service and keeps your tasks and their history.

Next: [Backups](/data/backups/index.html) · [Updates and channels](/maintain/updates/index.html) · [Calendar and reminders](/data/calendar/index.html)

# Shortcuts and Mac keys

One shortcut table drives every key BxRig binds, in two styles: Traditional (classic Super-key tiling) or Mac (Cmd-style keys).

## Try it

```bash
bxrig keys sheet                   # the shortcuts browser (Super+K)
bxrig tui shortcuts                # the same page in the Control Center
bxrig keys search screenshot       # find a shortcut by words, keys or id
bxrig keys style mac --yes         # switch to the Mac style
```

## The shortcuts browser

`Super+K` (or `bxrig keys sheet`) opens the Shortcuts page: every shortcut grouped under tabs (Editing, Apps, Windows and so on), the keys drawn as keycaps, and a detail pane that says how the shortcut is bound.

|              Key              |                                   What it does                                   |
|-------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `Left` `Right`, or `1` to `9` | Switch group                                                                     |
| `/` then type                 | Filter by action, keys, group or how it is bound (Enter keeps it, Esc clears it) |
| `u`                           | Show the shortcuts that have no keys too (they are hidden at first)              |
| `y`                           | Only your own shortcuts, marked with a star                                      |
| `a`                           | Back to everything                                                               |
| `e`, `r`, `c`                 | Rebind the highlighted one, reset it to the default, list conflicts              |

From a key binding it opens in its own terminal window. Without a terminal program it falls back to your menu program, grouped, with the keys written as `Super + Shift + T`.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["Shortcut table"] --> B["Traditional or Mac style"]
  B --> C["xremap: Cmd keys"]
  B --> D["Hyprland: bxrig.lua"]
  B --> E["Plasma"]
```

The table is `src/bxrig/Shortcuts.bx`. Every key BxRig binds is a row, including the window, workspace, arrow, mouse, volume and brightness keys, and each row has a key for each style. xremap is always installed: copy, paste, cut and select all (`Super+C V X A`) are remaps in both styles. Press `Super+K` to see every shortcut in your menu program.

## Change a shortcut

```bash
bxrig keys show                         # the table, in the style that is on
bxrig keys search screenshot           # find a shortcut by words, keys or id
bxrig keys run color-picker             # run the command a shortcut stands for
bxrig keys set ai-shell Super+Alt+A --yes
bxrig keys reset ai-shell --yes
bxrig keys conflicts                    # the table, the remaps of the style that is on, and your own hl.bind lines
```

Your changes live in `~/.config/bxrig/shortcuts.json` and apply to both styles. Remaps (the Cmd keys) are xremap's and cannot be changed this way. `keys set` refuses a key another binding uses or xremap rewrites.

## From the runner

`Super+Alt+Space` opens the menu; its Shortcuts section lists every shortcut, searches them (`bxrig keys search TEXT`), rebinds one (it asks which one and for the new keys, then runs `keys set`), runs the command a shortcut stands for (`bxrig keys run ID`), writes the keys to Hyprland and Plasma, and switches the style. `Super+Escape`, `Super+Ctrl+C`, `Super+Ctrl+O`, `Super+Ctrl+H` and `Super+Shift+Ctrl+A` open the System, Capture, Toggle, Hardware and Agent menus on their own (`bxrig menu open system`).

## Two styles

|                                                 |                  Traditional                  |                      Mac                      |
|-------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| Idea                                            | Classic Super-key tiling keys                 | Cmd-style keys for apps                       |
| `Super+C V X A`                                 | copy, paste, cut, select all (terminal aware) | same                                          |
| `Super+Z S F T N O P R W L B I U` and `Super+,` | plain Super keys                              | send the Ctrl version (Undo, Save, Find, ...) |
| Browser                                         | `Super+B`, `Super+Shift+Return`               | `Super+Shift+Return`                          |
| Private browser window                          | `Super+Alt+Shift+B`                           | `Super+Shift+N`                               |
| File manager                                    | `Super+Shift+F`                               | `Super+E`                                     |
| Full screen                                     | `Super+F`                                     | `Super+Ctrl+F`                                |
| Float or tile                                   | `Super+T`                                     | `Super+Alt+T`                                 |
| Window to workspace 3, 4, 5                     | `Super+Shift+3/4/5`                           | `Super+Alt+Shift+3/4/5`                       |

| `Print` (Mac style also `Super+Shift+3` / `4` / `5`)                         | Screenshot: region (Mac style: screen / region / menu)                                                                                                            |

| `Super+Ctrl+Comma`                                                           | Noctalia settings                                                                                                                                                 |

| `Super+Shift+Grave` / `Super+Ctrl+Grave`                                     | Quake console: show or hide / send the focused window there                                                                                                       |
| `Super+Alt+Shift+B` (Mac: `Super+Shift+N`)                                   | Private window of your default browser                                                                                                                            |
| `Super+Alt+Shift+F`                                                          | File manager in the folder of the focused window                                                                                                                  |
| `Super+Ctrl+F` (Mac: `Super+Ctrl+Shift+F`)                                   | Tiled full screen: the app goes full screen inside its tile                                                                                                       |
| `Super+Ctrl+Alt+Minus` / `Equal` (`Super+Alt+Shift+Minus` / `Equal`: height) | Floating window narrower / wider (shorter / taller)                                                                                                               |
| `Super+G` / `Super+Alt+G`                                                    | Group windows into tabs / take the window out of its group                                                                                                        |
| `Super+Alt+Tab` / `Super+Alt+Shift+Tab`                                      | Next / previous window in the group                                                                                                                               |

| `Super+Alt+8` / `Super+Alt+Equal` / `Super+Alt+Minus`                        | Zoom on or off / in / out, as Option+Cmd+8, = and - on a Mac. Off until `bxrig accessibility zoom on`                                                             |

| Play, Pause, Next, Previous keys                                             | Media control (playerctl)                                                                                                                                         |
| Keyboard backlight keys                                                      | Keyboard backlight up / down                                                                                                                                      |

## Advanced

On a PC keyboard the Mac style swaps Alt and Win (Alt acts as Cmd, Win as Option; the left keys only, Right Alt stays AltGr). An Apple keyboard never swaps. The choice is saved in `~/.config/bxrig/keystyle.json` (`bxrig keys style mac --keyboard=pc|apple --swap=on|off --yes`; the wizard asks the same). Keys in the table are what Hyprland sees after the swap, so with the swap on a PC keyboard `Super+Alt+D` is the Win and Alt keys in the places where Option and Cmd sit on a Mac. See `docs/architecture/SHORTCUTS-DECISIONS.md` for every decision.

Next: [The desktop](/desktop/desktop/index.html), [The menu](/desktop/menu/index.html), [Your own config](/customize/your-own-config/index.html).

# Your first hour

The wizard is done. This page shows what you have and what to try first. Each step takes a minute.

![BxRig: the default theme with its wallpaper, the bar and a themed terminal](/assets/screenshots/themes/bxrig.webp)

## What you got

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    R["BxRig"] --> D["Desktop: Hyprland and Noctalia, Plasma beside it"]
    R --> T["Toolchains: Java, BoxLang, MatchBox, Rust"]
    R --> A["Your apps from the catalog"]
    R --> AI["AI agents and local models"]
    R --> S["Safety: plans, backups, journal"]
    R --> C["One CLI: bxrig"]
```

Everything is also a command. `bxrig help` lists them all and every command takes `--json`.

## Try these

### 1. Open the control center

Press `Super+Space`. One search box finds apps, every setting and action, themes and the clipboard. `Super+Alt+Space` opens the same actions as a menu you browse by section.

![The launcher, in your theme's colours](/assets/screenshots/launcher-theme.webp)

Read more: [Control center and menu](/desktop/menu/index.html).

### 2. Find any shortcut

Press `Super+K` for the cheat sheet, or search by words:

```bash
bxrig keys search screenshot
```

Read more: [Shortcuts](/desktop/shortcuts/index.html).

### 3. Change the look

```bash
bxrig theme set tokyo-night
```

It changes at once: the bar, terminals, window borders and Neovim follow.

Read more: [Themes](/customize/themes/index.html), then [Appearance](/customize/appearance/index.html).

### 4. Look at your machine

```bash
bxrig status
bxrig tui
```

The terminal control center shows what needs attention and what is running.

![The Control Center dashboard](/assets/screenshots/control-center-dashboard.webp)

Read more: [Control Center](/desktop/control-center/index.html).

### 5. Install an app

```bash
bxrig tui apps
```

A catalog of about 290 apps by category. Read more: [Apps](/data/apps/index.html).

### 6. Start a BoxLang project

```bash
bxrig boxlang welcome
```

Read more: [BoxLang](/build/boxlang/index.html).

## If something is off

`bxrig status` shows what is missing, and each doctor prints a fix. See [Troubleshooting](/start/troubleshooting/index.html).

## Where next

Themes, bar, fonts, shortcuts and your own config files.

BxTimeMachine: setup snapshots, system snapshots and file backups.

Coding agents, local models and the tools they can use.

# Add an app

You will add one app, `lazydocker`, to the catalog. The catalog says what the app is. A small file per distribution says how to install it there.

## Files you touch

|                        File                        |                                                    What for                                                    |
|----------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `catalog/apps.json`                                | What the app is: name, group, category, tier, profiles. One entry.                                             |
| `catalog/install/arch.json`                        | How Arch and CachyOS install it.                                                                               |
| `catalog/install/suse.json`, `debian.json`         | Same for the other distributions (Ubuntu extends Debian). Skip a file and the app is simply not offered there. |
| `catalog/README.md`                                | The schema notes. Read it first, update it only if you add a field.                                            |
| `tests/catalog-test.sh`, `tests/catalog_check.bxs` | Run them. They fail when the catalog is inconsistent.                                                          |

## How an app reaches the user

This diagram shows how the two catalog files are merged and where the result is used.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["apps.json: what it is"] --> M["Catalog load: merge per distro"]
  B["install/DISTRO.json: how to install"] --> M
  M --> W["Wizard: Basic or Customize pages"]
  M --> P["Apps page, Discover tab"]
  M --> I["bxrig install"]
  M --> PL["Install plan: packages, repos, scripts"]
```

The Basic wizard choice installs every app with `tier: default`. The Customize choice shows one page per group, one list per category, with the default apps ticked. These pages are generated from the catalog, so a new app appears there with no wizard change.

## Steps

1. Add the entry to `apps` in `catalog/apps.json`. Pick an existing `group` and a `category` that belongs to that group.

   ```json
   {
     "id": "lazydocker",
     "name": "lazydocker",
     "description": "Terminal UI for Docker and Podman containers",
     "description_source": "curated",
     "kind": "tui",
     "group": "infra",
     "category": "Containers",
     "tier": "optional",
     "homepage": "https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazydocker",
     "macos": "lazydocker via Homebrew",
     "origin": ["owner-request"],
     "profiles": { "containers": "optional" }
   }
   ```

   * `kind` is `desktop`, `tui` or `web`.
   * `tier` is `default` (a plain install and the Basic wizard choice) or `optional` (offered in pickers).
   * `profiles` maps a profile id to `default` or `optional`. `bxrig profile-install containers` installs the `default` members, `--optional` adds the optional ones.
   * `shells: ["hyprland"]` limits the app to one desktop. Leave it out for both.
2. Add the install entry for each distribution that has it. For Arch, in `catalog/install/arch.json` under `apps`:

   ```json
   "lazydocker": {
     "source": "pacman",
     "targets": ["lazydocker"],
     "repo": "extra",
     "verified_on": "2026-11-27"
   }
   ```

   Sources on Arch: `pacman`, `aur`, `pkgbuild`, `script`, `flatpak`, `unresolved`. Debian and Ubuntu use `apt`, openSUSE uses `zypper`. `flatpak` and `script` work everywhere. `targets` are package names (or Flathub ids for `flatpak`).
3. A web app is different: `kind: "web"`, `source: "web"` and an `https` `url` in `apps.json`, and no install entry at all.

4. Let BxRig propose the other distributions' entries. Run this on that distribution:

   ```bash
   bxrig catalog map debian
   bxrig catalog map debian --write
   ```

## See it working

```bash
scripts/dev-build.sh
dist/bxrig catalog show lazydocker
dist/bxrig catalog check
dist/bxrig catalog coverage
dist/bxrig install lazydocker --dry-run
dist/bxrig tui apps            # Discover tab
```

`catalog check` prints every problem it finds and exits non-zero. `--distro=debian` on `show` and `list` shows another distribution's view.

## Test it

```bash
tests/catalog-test.sh dist/bxrig
```

The catalog schema checks (`Catalog.check`) run in the test and in `catalog check`. They reject, among others: an unknown group, a category that is not in the group, a missing description, an unsafe package name, a `pkgbuild` without a full 40 character commit, an unknown profile, a web app that has an install entry, and an install entry for an id that is not in `apps.json`.

## Common mistakes

* A `category` spelled differently from the one in `categories`: it must match the title exactly.
* Package names with spaces or shell characters: only letters, digits and `@ . _ + / : -` are allowed.
* A profile left with no `default` app on Arch: every profile needs at least one.
* An install entry for a web app, or for an id that is not in `apps.json`: both are errors.
* Editing only `arch.json`: the app is then offered on Arch only, which may be what you want.

## Advanced

* Install file keys: `distro`, `title`, `packager`, `extends`, `defaults`, `names` (Arch package name to this distribution's name, `""` when none is needed), `repos` (extra repositories added before a package in their `for` list) and `apps`.
* `provides` names the program a `script` app puts on the PATH, so a re-run is not treated as a new install. `conflicts` lists packages that cannot be installed beside this one: `bxrig install` skips the app and says why.
* `pkgbuild` apps need `repo`, `path` and a pinned `ref` (a full commit). `script` apps need an `https` `url`, optional `shell` (`sh` or `bash`) and `args`.
* Customize pages skip the categories the wizard asks about itself (shell, terminal, launchers, orchestration). See `src/bxrig/AppPages.bx` and `tests/app_pages_test.bxs`.
* Full schema notes: `catalog/README.md`. Next: [Wizard pages](/developer/wizard-pages/index.html), [Tests](/developer/tests/index.html).

body: Android apps BxRig can run Android apps next to your desktop apps with Waydroid : Android in a container, each app in its own window. It is off until you turn it on. A normal install and bxrig init do nothing about it (the wizard asks, and the answer is "Not now" unless you change it), and every command that changes something shows its plan first. Try it bxrig android # is it set up? is it running? does this machine support it? bxrig android setup # the plan: what would be installed and downloaded bxrig android setup --yes # do it (Google Play); --vanilla for no Google Check what you need A Wayland session. Hyprland is one, and so is Plasma on Wayland. An X11 session does not work. The kernel's binder driver. The CachyOS kernels have it. On another kernel, install binder_linux-dkms from the AUR and restart; BxRig never changes your kernel itself, and setup tells you when it is missing. Arch, CachyOS, Debian or Ubuntu. openSUSE has no Waydroid package, so BxRig does not offer Android there. About 1.2 GB of download for the image, and your password for the install. Set it up flowchart LR A["Add repo (Debian, Ubuntu)"] --> B["Install waydroid"] B --> C["Download Android image"] C --> D["Start waydroid-container"] D --> E["Start your Android session"] The diagram shows the steps bxrig android setup --yes runs. Each is shown in the plan before anything happens. On Debian and Ubuntu, add Waydroid's package repository ( repo.waydro.id ). Install waydroid (from the official repositories on Arch). Download the Android image: waydroid init -s GAPPS for Google Play, or -s VANILLA with --vanilla (LineageOS without Google). Start the waydroid-container service now and at every boot. Start your Android session. Run it again and it does only what is missing. With a different image than the one you have ( --vanilla over Google Play), it replaces the image and says so in the plan. Use it bxrig android apps # the Android apps installed bxrig android open # Android itself, full screen in a window bxrig android open Settings # an app: its name, a part of the name, or its package bxrig android install ~/Downloads/app.apk --yes bxrig android stop # stop the session (it frees the memory) bxrig android start Apps also appear in your applications menu once they are installed. An .apk has to support x86_64: one built only for arm will not run. F-Droid is a good place to get apps without Google. The Android page ( bxrig tui android ) shows the state first. While it is off, the page says so and S shows the plan to set it up. Once it is on it lists your Android apps: Enter opens one, s starts or stops Android, r registers it for Google Play. Fix "device not certified" Google Play shows "device not certified" until you register the device once: bxrig android register # prints this device's Android ID and where to register it bxrig android register --open # and opens that page in your browser Open Google Play once first, so the ID exists. Register the ID on your Google account at google.com/android/uncertified , give Google a few minutes, then bxrig android stop and bxrig android start . The vanilla image has no Google Play, so there is nothing to register. Take it out again bxrig android remove # the plan: stop it, disable the service, remove the package bxrig android remove --data --yes # and delete the images and everything in Android (apps, their data) Without --data the images and data stay on disk, so setting it up again is quick. Advanced Waydroid is also in the app catalog as an optional app on Arch ( bxrig install waydroid ), but bxrig android setup is the way to set it up properly. Next: Virtual machines · Apps and web apps

# Android apps

BxRig can run Android apps next to your desktop apps with [Waydroid](https://waydro.id): Android in a container, each app in its own window. **It is off until you turn it on.** A normal install and `bxrig init` do nothing about it (the wizard asks, and the answer is "Not now" unless you change it), and every command that changes something shows its plan first.

## Try it

```bash
bxrig android                       # is it set up? is it running? does this machine support it?
bxrig android setup                 # the plan: what would be installed and downloaded
bxrig android setup --yes           # do it (Google Play); --vanilla for no Google
```

## Check what you need

* **A Wayland session.** Hyprland is one, and so is Plasma on Wayland. An X11 session does not work.
* **The kernel's binder driver.** The CachyOS kernels have it. On another kernel, install `binder_linux-dkms` from the AUR and restart; BxRig never changes your kernel itself, and `setup` tells you when it is missing.
* **Arch, CachyOS, Debian or Ubuntu.** openSUSE has no Waydroid package, so BxRig does not offer Android there.
* About 1.2 GB of download for the image, and your password for the install.

## Set it up

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["Add repo (Debian, Ubuntu)"] --> B["Install waydroid"]
  B --> C["Download Android image"]
  C --> D["Start waydroid-container"]
  D --> E["Start your Android session"]
```

The diagram shows the steps `bxrig android setup --yes` runs. Each is shown in the plan before anything happens.

1. On Debian and Ubuntu, add Waydroid's package repository (`repo.waydro.id`).
2. Install `waydroid` (from the official repositories on Arch).
3. Download the Android image: `waydroid init -s GAPPS` for Google Play, or `-s VANILLA` with `--vanilla` (LineageOS without Google).
4. Start the `waydroid-container` service now and at every boot.
5. Start your Android session.

Run it again and it does only what is missing. With a different image than the one you have (`--vanilla` over Google Play), it replaces the image and says so in the plan.

## Use it

```bash
bxrig android apps                  # the Android apps installed
bxrig android open                  # Android itself, full screen in a window
bxrig android open Settings         # an app: its name, a part of the name, or its package
bxrig android install ~/Downloads/app.apk --yes
bxrig android stop                  # stop the session (it frees the memory)
bxrig android start
```

Apps also appear in your applications menu once they are installed. An `.apk` has to support x86_64: one built only for arm will not run. [F-Droid](https://f-droid.org) is a good place to get apps without Google.

The **Android** page (`bxrig tui android`) shows the state first. While it is off, the page says so and `S` shows the plan to set it up. Once it is on it lists your Android apps: `Enter` opens one, `s` starts or stops Android, `r` registers it for Google Play.

![The Android page of the Control Center](/assets/screenshots/android-page.webp)

## Fix "device not certified"

Google Play shows "device not certified" until you register the device once:

```bash
bxrig android register              # prints this device's Android ID and where to register it
bxrig android register --open       # and opens that page in your browser
```

Open Google Play once first, so the ID exists. Register the ID on your Google account at `google.com/android/uncertified`, give Google a few minutes, then `bxrig android stop` and `bxrig android start`. The vanilla image has no Google Play, so there is nothing to register.

## Take it out again

```bash
bxrig android remove                # the plan: stop it, disable the service, remove the package
bxrig android remove --data --yes   # and delete the images and everything in Android (apps, their data)
```

Without `--data` the images and data stay on disk, so setting it up again is quick.

## Advanced

Waydroid is also in the app catalog as an optional app on Arch (`bxrig install waydroid`), but `bxrig android setup` is the way to set it up properly.

Next: [Virtual machines](/build/databases-and-vms/index.html) · [Apps and web apps](/data/apps/index.html)
