title: Skills, MCP and agents
body: Skills, MCP and agents Three ways to let an AI agent work with BxRig. Pick the one you need. Recipe You write The agent gets A. Skill A SKILL.md Knowledge: which commands exist and when to use them. B. MCP tool One BoxLang function An action it can call, with approval for changes. C. BoxLang agent An agent project Its own assistant on your machine. This diagram shows how they connect: tools are written once and used by Boxy and by any other agent through MCP. flowchart LR S["Skill: SKILL.md"] --> AG["Any coding agent"] AG -- "MCP: bxrig mcp serve" --> T["Tools in tools/BxRig.bx"] BA["Boxy, a bx-agents agent"] --> T T --> C["bxrig COMMAND --json"] C --> D["The same plans and checks as the CLI"] A. Write an agent skill A skill is a Markdown file that tells an agent what BxRig can do. BxRig ships its own in skills/ , one folder each, and bxrig skills install bxrig stores them in ~/.agents/skills and links them into every agent you have. Files you touch: File What for skills/NAME/SKILL.md The skill. The folder name is the skill name. tests/skills-test.sh Lists the skill names it expects to be stored. Steps: Make the folder and file. Start with this frontmatter: name equals the folder name, and description says when to use the skill, because that is what the agent reads to decide. --- name: bxrig-example description: "Use this skill when the user asks about example things on a BxRig machine: the example command, its flags and when to run it." --- # BxRig: example - Show it: `bxrig example status [--json]`. - Change it: `bxrig example set VALUE --yes` (a plan is printed first without `--yes`). Keep it to real commands, one bullet each. Check each against bxrig help or the command reference . Say what needs --yes , since changes print a plan first. Add the name to the list in tests/skills-test.sh (the for n in bxrig bxrig-ai ... line). See it working: scripts/dev-build.sh dist/bxrig skills install bxrig --yes dist/bxrig skills installed dist/bxrig skills status Other useful commands: bxrig skills list , search TEXT , show OWNER/REPO/SLUG , update , remove NAME , link . Skills from the hub are checked by an audit, and one that fails it is refused. Test it: tests/skills-test.sh dist/bxrig . Common mistakes: a name that differs from the folder, a vague description , and commands that do not exist. B. Expose a tool over MCP bxrig mcp serve runs an MCP server whose tools are Boxy's tools. Each tool runs a BxRig command with --json , so an agent can do only what BxRig does. Add a tool once and both Boxy and every linked agent get it. Files you touch: File What for templates/agents/boxy/tools/BxRig.bx One function per tool, marked @AITool . templates/agents/boxy/Agent.bx NEEDS_OK : the tools that change something and need approval. tests/mcp_test.bxs Counts the tools (36) and the changing ones (19). Update both numbers. docs/ai/boxlang-agents.md The "36 tools" sentence. Steps: Add a function to BxRig.bx . The @AITool text is what the model reads, and the DocBox @param lines describe the arguments. The private bxrig() helper appends --json , runs the command and returns the data. /** * Shows the uptime of this machine. * * @return The command's answer as JSON text for the model. */ @AITool( "How long this machine has been running." ) function uptime_status() { return bxrig( [ "system", "uptime" ] ); } If the tool changes something, add its name to NEEDS_OK in Agent.bx . Such a tool waits for a person's OK and passes --yes , because the plan was the approval. Read-only tools need nothing. Update the counts in tests/mcp_test.bxs . See it working: dist/bxrig mcp tools # your tool is listed, marked if it changes something dist/bxrig mcp link claude-code --yes # read-only; add --write to allow changes dist/bxrig mcp # who is linked bxrig mcp link [AGENT...] writes the agent's own config (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Cursor, Zed, VS Code and more) and unlink takes it out. Without --write the changing tools are off. Test it: (cd src && matchbox ../tests/mcp_test.bxs) and tests/mcp-test.sh dist/bxrig . Common mistakes: a tool that calls something other than a bxrig command, a changing tool missing from NEEDS_OK (it would run without asking), and forgetting the counts. C. Build a BoxLang agent bx-agents builds agents in BoxLang. BxRig installs it, keeps your agent projects in ~/Agents , runs each as a user service and can point it at your local model. Boxy, BxRig's own assistant, is such an agent: its source is templates/agents/boxy/ ( Agent.bx , instructions.md , tools/BxRig.bx ). Steps: Install and create. bxrig ai agents install --yes bxrig ai agents new Helper --model=openai-compatible/qwen3.5-0.8b --no-wizard Edit the project in ~/Agents/Helper : instructions.md for behavior, tools/ for what it can do, Agent.bx for the model. A tool is a BoxLang class with @AITool functions, like step B. For changes that need approval, use the same pattern as Boxy: a NEEDS_OK list and HumanInTheLoopMiddleware in Agent.bx . /** * Helper: a bx-agents agent that keeps its changing tools behind a person's OK. */ class extends="bxModules.bxai.models.runnables.AiAgent" { variables.NEEDS_OK = [ "my_changing_tool" ]; /** * Builds the agent and puts the approval middleware in front of the changing tools. * * @return The agent. */ function init() { super.init( name : "Helper", description : "What it is for" ) withCheckpointer( aiMemory( memory : "cache", config : {} ) ) withMiddleware( new bxModules.bxai.models.middleware.core.HumanInTheLoopMiddleware( toolsRequiringApproval = variables.NEEDS_OK, mode : "web" ) ) return this } } Run it. bxrig ai agents start Helper bxrig ai agents ask Helper what can you do bxrig ai agents open Helper See BoxLang agents for all the commands: stop, default, approve, skills review, and every bxAgents verb through bxrig ai agents NAME VERB . Note: The bxrig profile in ~/.bxagents/Agent.yml points agents at your local model. Change configure() in Agent.bx to use another provider. Advanced The MCP server is written to ~/.local/share/bxrig/mcp from templates/mcp/serve.bxs and runs on BoxLang with bx-ai (installed by bx-agents). NEEDS_OK is read from Agent.bx text, so keep its one-array-of-strings shape. Tool output is cut at 6000 characters before it goes to the model. Skills saved by an agent while it works are listed with bxrig ai agents skills and wait for your review. Next: Add a command , Tests .

# Skills, MCP and agents

Three ways to let an AI agent work with BxRig. Pick the one you need.

|                    Recipe                    |      You write       |                    The agent gets                     |
|----------------------------------------------|----------------------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| [A. Skill](#a-write-an-agent-skill)          | A `SKILL.md`         | Knowledge: which commands exist and when to use them. |
| [B. MCP tool](#b-expose-a-tool-over-mcp)     | One BoxLang function | An action it can call, with approval for changes.     |
| [C. BoxLang agent](#c-build-a-boxlang-agent) | An agent project     | Its own assistant on your machine.                    |

This diagram shows how they connect: tools are written once and used by Boxy and by any other agent through MCP.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  S["Skill: SKILL.md"] --> AG["Any coding agent"]
  AG -- "MCP: bxrig mcp serve" --> T["Tools in tools/BxRig.bx"]
  BA["Boxy, a bx-agents agent"] --> T
  T --> C["bxrig COMMAND --json"]
  C --> D["The same plans and checks as the CLI"]
```

## A. Write an agent skill

A skill is a Markdown file that tells an agent what BxRig can do. BxRig ships its own in `skills/`, one folder each, and `bxrig skills install bxrig` stores them in `~/.agents/skills` and links them into every agent you have.

Files you touch:

|          File          |                    What for                    |
|------------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| `skills/NAME/SKILL.md` | The skill. The folder name is the skill name.  |
| `tests/skills-test.sh` | Lists the skill names it expects to be stored. |

Steps:

1. Make the folder and file. Start with this frontmatter: `name` equals the folder name, and `description` says when to use the skill, because that is what the agent reads to decide.

   ```markdown
   ---
   name: bxrig-example
   description: "Use this skill when the user asks about example things on a BxRig machine: the example command, its flags and when to run it."
   ---

   # BxRig: example

   - Show it: `bxrig example status [--json]`.
   - Change it: `bxrig example set VALUE --yes` (a plan is printed first without `--yes`).
   ```

2. Keep it to real commands, one bullet each. Check each against `bxrig help` or [the command reference](/reference/commands/index.html). Say what needs `--yes`, since changes print a plan first.

3. Add the name to the list in `tests/skills-test.sh` (the `for n in bxrig bxrig-ai ...` line).

See it working:

```bash
scripts/dev-build.sh
dist/bxrig skills install bxrig --yes
dist/bxrig skills installed
dist/bxrig skills status
```

Other useful commands: `bxrig skills list`, `search TEXT`, `show OWNER/REPO/SLUG`, `update`, `remove NAME`, `link`. Skills from the hub are checked by an audit, and one that fails it is refused.

Test it: `tests/skills-test.sh dist/bxrig`.

Common mistakes: a `name` that differs from the folder, a vague `description`, and commands that do not exist.

## B. Expose a tool over MCP

`bxrig mcp serve` runs an MCP server whose tools are Boxy's tools. Each tool runs a BxRig command with `--json`, so an agent can do only what BxRig does. Add a tool once and both Boxy and every linked agent get it.

Files you touch:

|                  File                  |                                What for                                |
|----------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `templates/agents/boxy/tools/BxRig.bx` | One function per tool, marked `@AITool`.                               |
| `templates/agents/boxy/Agent.bx`       | `NEEDS_OK`: the tools that change something and need approval.         |
| `tests/mcp_test.bxs`                   | Counts the tools (36) and the changing ones (19). Update both numbers. |
| `docs/ai/boxlang-agents.md`            | The "36 tools" sentence.                                               |

Steps:

1. Add a function to `BxRig.bx`. The `@AITool` text is what the model reads, and the DocBox `@param` lines describe the arguments. The private `bxrig()` helper appends `--json`, runs the command and returns the data.

   ```boxlang
   /**
    * Shows the uptime of this machine.
    *
    * @return The command's answer as JSON text for the model.
    */
   @AITool( "How long this machine has been running." )
   function uptime_status() { return bxrig( [ "system", "uptime" ] ); }
   ```

2. If the tool changes something, add its name to `NEEDS_OK` in `Agent.bx`. Such a tool waits for a person's OK and passes `--yes`, because the plan was the approval. Read-only tools need nothing.

3. Update the counts in `tests/mcp_test.bxs`.

See it working:

```bash
dist/bxrig mcp tools                       # your tool is listed, marked if it changes something
dist/bxrig mcp link claude-code --yes      # read-only; add --write to allow changes
dist/bxrig mcp                             # who is linked
```

`bxrig mcp link [AGENT...]` writes the agent's own config (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Cursor, Zed, VS Code and more) and `unlink` takes it out. Without `--write` the changing tools are off. Test it: `(cd src && matchbox ../tests/mcp_test.bxs)` and `tests/mcp-test.sh dist/bxrig`.

Common mistakes: a tool that calls something other than a `bxrig` command, a changing tool missing from `NEEDS_OK` (it would run without asking), and forgetting the counts.

## C. Build a BoxLang agent

[bx-agents](https://bxagents.ai) builds agents in BoxLang. BxRig installs it, keeps your agent projects in `~/Agents`, runs each as a user service and can point it at your local model. Boxy, BxRig's own assistant, is such an agent: its source is `templates/agents/boxy/` (`Agent.bx`, `instructions.md`, `tools/BxRig.bx`).

Steps:

1. Install and create.

   ```bash
   bxrig ai agents install --yes
   bxrig ai agents new Helper --model=openai-compatible/qwen3.5-0.8b --no-wizard
   ```

2. Edit the project in `~/Agents/Helper`: `instructions.md` for behavior, `tools/` for what it can do, `Agent.bx` for the model.

3. A tool is a BoxLang class with `@AITool` functions, like step B. For changes that need approval, use the same pattern as Boxy: a `NEEDS_OK` list and `HumanInTheLoopMiddleware` in `Agent.bx`.

   ```boxlang
   /**
    * Helper: a bx-agents agent that keeps its changing tools behind a person's OK.
    */
   class extends="bxModules.bxai.models.runnables.AiAgent" {
   	variables.NEEDS_OK = [ "my_changing_tool" ];

   	/**
   	 * Builds the agent and puts the approval middleware in front of the changing tools.
   	 *
   	 * @return The agent.
   	 */
   	function init() {
   		super.init( name : "Helper", description : "What it is for" )
   		withCheckpointer( aiMemory( memory : "cache", config : {} ) )
   		withMiddleware( new bxModules.bxai.models.middleware.core.HumanInTheLoopMiddleware(
   			toolsRequiringApproval = variables.NEEDS_OK, mode : "web" ) )
   		return this
   	}
   }
   ```

4. Run it.

   ```bash
   bxrig ai agents start Helper
   bxrig ai agents ask Helper what can you do
   bxrig ai agents open Helper
   ```

See [BoxLang agents](/ai/boxlang-agents/index.html) for all the commands: stop, default, approve, skills review, and every `bxAgents` verb through `bxrig ai agents NAME VERB`.
> **Note:** The `bxrig` profile in `~/.bxagents/Agent.yml` points agents at your local model. Change `configure()` in `Agent.bx` to use another provider.

## Advanced

* The MCP server is written to `~/.local/share/bxrig/mcp` from `templates/mcp/serve.bxs` and runs on BoxLang with bx-ai (installed by bx-agents). `NEEDS_OK` is read from `Agent.bx` text, so keep its one-array-of-strings shape.
* Tool output is cut at 6000 characters before it goes to the model.
* Skills saved by an agent while it works are listed with `bxrig ai agents skills` and wait for your review.
* Next: [Add a command](/developer/add-a-command/index.html), [Tests](/developer/tests/index.html).

Without unicode every style is ascii. Meter : label , message , unit( "bytes" ) (sizes and speeds as 1.4 MB and 3.2 MB/s ), style , gradient , color , width , total (when the size becomes known), advance , set , template , draw , finish , and ratio() , rate() (over the last updates), eta() , elapsed() . Multi keeps a finished meter's line with a check mark. One call, two outputs Commands built on Out get a styled block for people and data for --json from one call: out.table( "Java", columns, rows, asJson, { total: rows.len() } ) // text: the table; --json: { rows: [...], total } out.kv( "Status", { jenv: "ready", global: "21" }, asJson ) out.blocks( data, asJson, ui.panel( "Done" ) ) Tests: tests/ui_test.bxs (golden output, widths 40, 80 and 120, plain and colour). Help pages bxrig help , bxrig --help and bxrig COMMAND --help are drawn with this toolkit ( bxrig.Help ): the DOS Rebel wordmark in the brand gradient and a version badge on a terminal, an UPPERCASE coloured title per group, a bold command name and one dim line each (the brief of the command in docs/reference/cli.json , at most 60 characters, checked by bootstrap/gen-docs.sh ). A command page has USAGE (one form per line, narrowed by the words after the command: bxrig ai models --help ), FLAGS, EXAMPLES and NOTES. A usage error prints the forms one per line too ( CommandSpec.usage ). Piped output has no colour and no wordmark.
markdown:
# The terminal UI toolkit (`bxrig.ui`)

New to it? When your command prints something for people, do not join strings by hand. Ask the toolkit for a table, a panel or a status line and print the result. It handles color, width and plain output for you, and the same call gives data for `--json`.

This diagram shows the path from your data to the screen or to a pipe.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  D["Your rows or values"] --> U["bxrig.ui helper"]
  U --> T{"Terminal?"}
  T -->|"yes"| C["Color, unicode, width"]
  T -->|"piped or NO_COLOR"| P["Plain text"]
  D --> O["Out: --json data"]
```

Commands that print (not the full-screen TUI) build their output with `bxrig.ui`. One call gives tables, panels, badges, key-value lists, trees, columns, status lines, progress bars, sparklines, bar charts, step checklists, gradients and hyperlinks. Every helper returns text or an array of lines; nothing prints until you call `print`.

```boxlang
ui = new bxrig.ui.Ui();
ui.print( ui.table(
    [ { key: "id", title: "Major", align: "right" }, { key: "name", title: "Name" }, "vendor" ],
    rows, { title: "Java" } ) );
ui.print( ui.panel( "Saved the keys.", { title: "Done", border: "ok" } ) );
```

## Terminal rules

`Term` decides once: colour only on a terminal, never with `NO_COLOR`, `TERM=dumb` or `plain`; truecolor from `COLORTERM`, else the nearest of 256 colours; unicode from the locale (ASCII borders and glyphs otherwise); width from `COLUMNS` or `stty`, else 80, never below 20. With colour off every style call returns the plain text, so piped output is clean. Tests force all of it: `new bxrig.ui.Ui( { color: true, truecolor: true, width: 60, unicode: true } )`.

Widths are measured as the screen shows them: escapes take no room, wide characters (日本語, 😀) two columns, combining marks none.

## Colours

A colour is a role (`accent accent2 ok warn err info text dim border header zebra`), a basic name (`red cyan gray ...`) or a hex like `#00c8ff`. A style is words: `bold dim italic underline inverse strike`, a colour, `bg:COLOUR`.

```boxlang
ui.style( "installed", "bold ok" )
ui.style( " LTS ", "bold black bg:warn" )
ui.colors( { accent: "#ff8800" } )   // change a role, for example to the theme that is on
```

## The helpers

|                                       Call                                        |                                                                                                                                                                        Result                                                                                                                                                                        |
|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `ui.table( columns, rows, opts )`                                                 | A table. Columns: `key title align width min max grow wrap format style`. Options: `border` (`rounded plain heavy double ascii none`), `title`, `footer`, `zebra`, `rowLines`, `width`, `padding`, `empty`, `fill`. A table wider than the terminal shrinks its widest columns first and cuts text with an ellipsis, or wraps a `wrap: true` column. |
| `ui.panel( content, opts )`                                                       | A box with `title`, `subtitle`, `border`, `color`, `padding`, `width`, `fill`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `ui.callout( kind, text, opts )`                                                  | A coloured bar with wrapped text (`ok warn err info`).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| `ui.section( title, blurb )`, `ui.rule( title )`                                  | An UPPERCASE heading; a rule with a title in it.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `ui.kv( pairs, opts )`                                                            | Aligned label and value lines, values wrapped with a hanging indent.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `ui.list( items, opts )`, `ui.tree( nodes )`                                      | Bullets or numbers with children; a tree with `├─ └─ │`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `ui.beside( blocks, opts )`                                                       | Blocks (arrays of lines) side by side.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| `ui.columns( items, format, opts )`                                               | A list of simple values in columns filled top to bottom, from the widest item and the terminal width (like `ls`). `format( item, row, column )` returns a format such as `"blue"`.                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `ui.treeOf( data, format )`                                                       | A tree from nested structs (a key with a struct is a branch, `""` or `{}` a leaf). `format( pathString, pathArray )` returns a format.                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| `ui.badge( text, role )`, `ui.pill( text, role )`, `ui.status( kind, text )`      | Small marks: `[LTS]`, `✓ installed`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `ui.bar( ratio, width, opts )`, `ui.spark( values )`, `ui.barChart( rows, opts )` | Progress bar, sparkline, horizontal bar chart.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `ui.steps( items, opts )`, `ui.spinner().frame( tick )`                           | A step checklist; a spinner frame.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `ui.live()`                                                                       | A block that redraws itself in place (`update( lines )`, `finish()`).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `ui.gradient( text )`, `ui.link( text, url )`                                     | A gradient across the text; an OSC 8 hyperlink.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `ui.truncate`, `ui.align`, `ui.wrap`, `ui.textWidth`, `ui.strip`                  | Text helpers that know about escapes and wide characters.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |

## The fluent print helper

`ui.printer()` returns a buffer you chain calls on, after CommandBox's `print`. **Any method name is a format**:

```boxlang
p = ui.printer();
p.boldGreenText( "Installed" ).line()
 .redOnWhiteLine( "ERROR" )
 .indentedLine( "detail" )
 .text( status, status == "running" ? "green" : "red" )   // a format chosen at run time
 .table( rows ).columns( names, ( item, row, col ) => "blue" ).tree( data )
 .toConsole();
```

Rules: a colour name colours the text (`red`, `accent`, `ok`, `color221`, the xterm numbers; also `maroon olive navy silver lime fuchsia aqua`, `orange pink gold ...`), `on` + a colour is the background, decorations are `bold dim italic underscored underline blinking reversed concealed strike`, `indented` puts two spaces before every line, and `line` ends the text with a line break. Other words (`text`, `and`, `background`) are ignored so a name reads well. A second string is added to the name, so `p.text( s, "green" )` is `p.greenText( s )`.

* `toConsole()` prints and clears the buffer; `toString()` and `lines()` return it; `unANSI( s )` strips escapes.
* `table( data, includeHeaders, headerNames, debug, options )` takes what CommandBox's `print.table` takes: arrays of arrays or of structs, a cell can be `{ value, options: "blueOnWhite" }`, columns shrink to fit, and a terminal too narrow for them gets one `...` column in place of the right-hand ones.
* `columns( items, format )` and `tree( data, format )` are CommandBox's `print.columns` and `print.tree`.
* `panel`, `callout`, `section`, `rule`, `kv`, `list`, `beside`, `steps`, `barChart`, `gauge`, `tabs` and `paragraph` add the same blocks as the toolkit.

The toolkit itself speaks the same language and returns a styled string: `ui.boldRed( "failed" )`, `ui.greenOnBlack( "ok" )`, `ui.text( s, "magenta" )`. With colour off they return the text unchanged. (A misspelt method on `Ui` or `Print` is read as a format and does not raise an error.)

`ui.styled()` builds a reusable style by chaining: `warn = ui.styled().boldYellow(); warn.apply( "careful" )`; `copy()` and `patch()` combine styles.

## Progress bars

`ui.bar( ratio, width, opts )` draws a bar; `ui.meter( total )` tracks a task with a rate and an ETA; `ui.multi()` stacks several meters under one display.

```boxlang
ui.bar( 0.62, 40, { style: "smooth", gradient: true } )            // █████████████████████████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░  62%
ui.indeterminate( tick, 40 )                                        // a bright stretch that moves back and forth
ui.segments( [ { label: "System", value: 41 }, { label: "Free", value: 59 } ], 60, { format: v => v & " GB" } )

m = ui.meter( 480000000 ).label( "Downloading Java 25" ).unit( "bytes" ).gradient();
m.advance( chunk ).draw();                                          // ⠋ Downloading Java 25 ███████▌░░░ 31% 148 MB/458 MB 95 MB/s ETA 3s
m.finish( "Installed" );

mp = ui.multi();  java = mp.add( 480, "Java 25" ).unit( "bytes" );  node = mp.add( 120, "Node 24" ).style( "line" );
java.advance( 60 );  mp.draw();
```

* **Styles** (`style`): `smooth` (partial blocks, an eighth of a cell), `line` (thick and thin line), `blocks`, `thin`, `dots`, `braille`, `arrow` (`[====>----]`) and `ascii`. Without unicode every style is ascii.
* **Colour** : `role` for one colour, or `gradient: true` (accent to accent2) or `gradient: [ "ok", "info" ]`, spread over the whole bar so the colour at a cell never changes as it fills. `track` colours the empty part. `ends: "[]"`, `percent`, `label`.
* **Meter** : `label`, `message`, `unit( "bytes" )` (sizes and speeds as `1.4 MB` and `3.2 MB/s`), `style`, `gradient`, `color`, `width`, `total` (when the size becomes known), `advance`, `set`, `template`, `draw`, `finish`, and `ratio()`, `rate()` (over the last updates), `eta()`, `elapsed()`. The default template follows the unit and fits the terminal: the bar takes what the other tokens leave. A template uses `{spinner} {label} {bar} {bar:30} {pos} {total} {percent} {rate} {eta} {elapsed} {message} {bytes} {total_bytes}`. A task with no total shows the elapsed time and a moving bar.
* **In place or in a log** : on a colour terminal `draw()` redraws one line (a `Live`); elsewhere it prints a line each time the percent moves 10 points, so a log stays short. `Multi` keeps a finished meter's line with a check mark.
* **Spinners** : `ui.spinner().frame( tick, "accent", "arc" )`; sixteen sets (`dots dots2 line arc bounce arrows pulse grow box triangle square hamburger star toggle balloon rain`).
* **Time** : pass `clock: function() { return ms; }` to `meter()` or `multi()` to test without the real clock.

## Ideas taken from ratatui

|                                         Call                                          |                                                         Result                                                         |
|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `ui.spans( [ "Installed ", [ "Java 21", "boldGreen" ], " in ", [ "41 s", "dim" ] ] )` | Styled parts joined into one string (ratatui's `Span` and `Line`).                                                     |
| `ui.paragraph( text, { width, align, wrap, indent, style } )`                         | Text laid out in a width, left, centred or right.                                                                      |
| `ui.layout( [ "length:10", "fill", "percentage:25", "max:8" ], width, gap )`          | The widths of a split: `length`, `percentage`, `ratio:1/3`, `min`, `max`, `fill:2` (a weighted share of what is left). |
| `ui.split( blocks, constraints, opts )`                                               | Blocks placed side by side in those widths.                                                                            |
| `ui.gauge( ratio, { width, label, role } )`                                           | A full-width bar with the label inside it.                                                                             |
| `ui.lineGauge( ratio, { width } )`                                                    | `50% ━━━━━━━━━━──────────`                                                                                             |
| `ui.tabs( titles, selected )`                                                         | A row of titles with the selected one marked.                                                                          |
| `ui.panel( content, { borders: "top,bottom", titleAlign: "right" } )`                 | A block with only the borders you list, and titles at the left, centre or right.                                       |
| `ui.list( items, { selected: 2 } )`                                                   | A list with a highlighted row and its symbol.                                                                          |

## One call, two outputs

Commands built on `Out` get a styled block for people and data for `--json` from one call:

```boxlang
out.table( "Java", columns, rows, asJson, { total: rows.len() } )   // text: the table; --json: { rows: [...], total }
out.kv( "Status", { jenv: "ready", global: "21" }, asJson )
out.blocks( data, asJson, ui.panel( "Done" ) )
```

Tests: `tests/ui_test.bxs` (golden output, widths 40, 80 and 120, plain and colour).

## Help pages

`bxrig help`, `bxrig --help` and `bxrig COMMAND --help` are drawn with this toolkit (`bxrig.Help`): the DOS Rebel wordmark in the brand gradient and a version badge on a terminal, an UPPERCASE coloured title per group, a bold command name and one dim line each (the `brief` of the command in `docs/reference/cli.json`, at most 60 characters, checked by `bootstrap/gen-docs.sh`). A command page has USAGE (one form per line, narrowed by the words after the command: `bxrig ai models --help`), FLAGS, EXAMPLES and NOTES. A usage error prints the forms one per line too (`CommandSpec.usage`). Piped output has no colour and no wordmark.

# Tests

Tests never touch your real machine. They run the program against fake tools in a scratch folder, so they need no root and no network.

## Run them

```bash
tests/run-all.sh                          # every test (JOBS=3 in parallel by default)
tests/run-all.sh dist/bxrig theme         # only tests whose name contains "theme"
bash tests/time-test.sh dist/bxrig        # one shell test
tests/run-all.sh dist/bxrig init_plan     # one .bxs test (runs from source, no build)
bash tests/dry-test.sh                    # the ratchet
```

Rebuild with `scripts/dev-build.sh` first: shell tests run `dist/bxrig`. The `.bxs` tests run from `src/` and need no build.
> **Tip:** `wizard-test` is timing sensitive. If it fails, run it alone with `JOBS=1 tests/run-all.sh dist/bxrig wizard`.

## Two kinds of test

|    Kind    |         File          |                    Runs                     |                                Use it for                                 |
|------------|-----------------------|---------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Shell test | `tests/NAME-test.sh`  | The built binary, with fake tools on `PATH` | A command end to end: exit codes, plan, `--json`, which tools were called |
| Unit test  | `tests/NAME_test.bxs` | `matchbox` from `src/`, no build            | A class or helper on its own                                              |

`tests/run-all.sh` finds both by name. `native-package-integration.sh` is skipped (it needs a sandbox); `tests/arch/` holds the real-pacman suite.

## Write a shell test

A test starts by sourcing the harness. The harness gives you `binary`, `root`, `tmp` (a scratch folder removed on exit), `fail`, `stub` and `code`.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# `bxrig dnsflush` with a fake resolvectl. Usage: dnsflush-test.sh BINARY
. "$(dirname "$0")/lib/harness.sh"
export LOG="$tmp/log"; : > "$LOG"
stub resolvectl 'echo "resolvectl $*" >> "$LOG"'
run() { env HOME="$tmp/home" PATH="$tmp/bin:$PATH" LOG="$LOG" "$@"; }

[[ "$(code "$binary" dnsflush)" == 2 ]] || fail 'without --yes it is a plan'
run "$binary" dnsflush --yes >/dev/null
grep -qF 'resolvectl flush-caches' "$LOG" || fail 'the flush did not run'
```

1. **Fake the tools.** `stub NAME 'bash body'` writes an executable into `$tmp/bin`. Log each call to a file and assert on the log.
2. **Define `run()`.** It sets the environment: `HOME`, `PATH="$tmp/bin:$PATH"` and any `BXRIG_*` override (for example `BXRIG_CONFIG_HOME`, `BXRIG_STATE_HOME`). The list of overrides is in `Env.names()`.
3. **Assert exit codes with `code`.** `code CMD...` prints the exit code of `run CMD...`.
4. **Check `--json` with `jq -e`.** Assert on `.ok`, `.exit`, `.dry_run` and `.data`.
5. **Prove a plan changed nothing.** Check the fake zone file or the log is untouched after a run without `--yes`.
6. **List it in CI.** See below.

Helpers in `tests/lib/harness.sh`:

|            Helper            |                                 What it does                                  |
|------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `stub NAME BODY`             | An executable `$tmp/bin/NAME` with that bash body.                            |
| `stub_id`                    | `id -u` answers 1000 (`MOCK_UID` changes it).                                 |
| `stub_sudo`, `stub_sudo_log` | `sudo` runs the command; the log variant records `sudo ARGS` in `$LOG` first. |
| `code CMD...`                | The exit code of `run CMD...`, output hidden.                                 |
| `fail MSG`                   | Print `FAIL: MSG` and exit 1.                                                 |

The harness also unsets the `XDG_*` variables and sets `BXRIG_DISTRO=arch`, so a CI runner behaves like the Arch the tests describe. Do not define `fail`, `code` or the temp-dir trap again in a test.

## Write a unit test

Unit tests use `lib.Check` (`tests/lib/Check.bx`) and run from `src/`.

```boxlang
testkit = new lib.Check( "out" );
cli = new bxrig.util.Cli( "0.0.0" );
testkit.check( "Out.usage is 2", cli.scoped( "demo" ).usage( "bad", false ) == 2 );
testkit.done();
```

`check( label, ok )` prints `ok` or `FAIL` lines, `tmp()` gives a scratch folder, and `done()` exits 1 when anything failed. Run it with `(cd src && matchbox ../tests/NAME_test.bxs)`. Tests (`*.bxs`) do not need DocBox comments.

## Every test is listed in CI

`tests/dry-test.sh` fails when a `*-test.sh` or `*_test.bxs` file is not named in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, and when a tracked `*.sh` is missing from CI's `bash -n` list. So a new test needs two edits in `ci.yml`: a run line (shell tests use `bash tests/NAME-test.sh "$candidate"`, unit tests `(cd src && matchbox ../tests/NAME_test.bxs)`) and, for a shell test, its name in the `bash -n` list.

## Advanced

### The ratchet

`tests/dry-test.sh` counts banned patterns (a command class that defines its own `say`, `fail` or `has`, hand-written "Nothing was changed" footers, bare exit numbers, `getSystemSetting` outside `Env`, `pacman` or `curl` argv lists outside `util/`). Each has a maximum that only goes down. When a refactor removes copies, the script prints `note: ... lower the maximum` and you lower it. Never raise one. It also runs `scripts/format.sh --check`.

### What every changing command should test

From the [contract](/architecture/COMMAND-CONTRACT/index.html) (section 7): success, no-op, invalid input, dependency failure, privilege rejection, partial failure and recovery. Cases that need KDE, Wayland or real hardware are marked manual.

### Speed

Shell tests start the native binary for each call, so keep the number of calls small. For logic with many cases, prefer a `.bxs` unit test.

# Code rules

The code review of 2026-11-14 ([CODE-REVIEW](/architecture/CODE-REVIEW/index.html)) found the same helper pasted into 20 to 57 classes. These rules keep that from coming back.

Rules marked **(ratchet)** are enforced by `bash tests/dry-test.sh`: each banned pattern has a maximum count that only goes down.
> **Note:** The rule numbers are the original ones; the page groups them by theme.
> **Tip:** Before you write a helper, run `grep -rn "function NAME" src/`. If it exists anywhere, use it or move it. Never paste it.

## Reuse before you write

**1. One home per concept.**
Why: ten copies means ten bugs.

**2. A command class never defines `say`, `fail`, `tryExec`, `has`, `env`, `home`, `self` or `merge` (ratchet).**
Why: each already has one home. Use `Cli`/`Out` for output, `Proc` for processes, `Env` for paths and variables, `Text` for strings.

**5. Parse each format once.**
Why: parsers drift apart. `.desktop` files go through `DesktopEntry` (parse, folders, entries, render).

The shared helpers are in `src/bxrig/util/`: `Cli`, `Out`, `Exit`, `Mutation`, `Proc`, `Env`, `Text`, `Fmt`, `Names`, `JsonStore`, `SystemFile`, `SystemdUnit`, `Systemd`, `Pacman`, `Aur`, `Http`, `Urls`, `Desktop`, `DesktopEntry`, `Ini`, `Props`, `Lua`, `Version`. The terminal UI helpers are `Modal`, `KeyMap` and `IntentRunner`. Copy what they do, not the old copies.

## Paths, processes and files

**3. Never read `HOME`, `XDG_*` or `BXRIG_*_HOME` directly. Ask `Env`.**
Why: one precedence everywhere: `BXRIG_*_HOME`, then `XDG_*_HOME`, then the default under `$HOME`. A new test override is added to `Env` and listed in [config files](/reference/config-files/index.html).

```boxlang
// yes
path = new bxrig.util.Env().config( "worldclock.json" );
// no
path = getSystemSetting( "HOME" ) & "/.config/bxrig/worldclock.json";
```

**4. Run programs only through `Proc`, with an argv array.**
Why: no shell string means no injection and one place to fake in tests. "Is it installed" is `Proc.has`; `Proc.works` is only for version checks.

**15. Start a program in the background with `Proc.detach`** , not another `setsid` string.
Why: one tested way to detach.

**7. Every file BxRig writes goes through `ConfigService`.**
Why: it gives backup, atomic replace and a journal, so `config restore` works. The config folder comes from `Env`.

## Commands and output

**6. Name exit codes by intent.**
Why: a typo must not become a wrong exit code. Use `out.usage` (2), `out.precondition` (4), `out.failed` (6). Do not invent new codes: the table in the [command contract](/architecture/COMMAND-CONTRACT/index.html) is the only list. An unknown command or flag exits 2.

**12. A new command is an entry in `docs/reference/cli.json` and a `case` in `src/Main.bx`.**
Why: `gen-docs.sh` fails when the two disagree. Usage text is `new bxrig.CommandSpec().usage( "name" )`, never a string. See [Add a command](/developer/add-a-command/index.html).

**13. Plans and dry runs are `Out.plan` (`util/Mutation`) (ratchet).**
Why: the wording and exit code are part of the contract. Write "Nothing was changed" nowhere else. A command that changes none of your files and only starts a program or flips your own setting acts at once and documents it.

**14. A key is a row of the one table in `Shortcuts.bx`** , with a Traditional and a Mac key.
Why: both styles must stay in sync. Run `keys conflicts` in both styles (`tests/shortcuts_test.bxs` does). A key that runs a command is `bx( ... )` with the words after `bxrig`, so `keys run ID` and the runner can run it, and the command gets a runner entry in `MenuTree`. See [Add a shortcut](/developer/add-a-shortcut/index.html).

## Data and generated files

**10. Data files are resources; a few files are generated.**
Why: edit data in place, regenerate only what is generated.

|   Kind    |                                                                Files                                                                |                                        What you do                                         |
|-----------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Resource  | catalog, templates, themes, skills, wizard pages, brand images, `cli.json` (from `src/resources/`, which links to the real folders) | Edit the file. Nothing to regenerate.                                                      |
| Generated | `Version.bx`, `WallpaperData.bx`, `CommandFlagData.bx`, `docs/reference/commands.md`, `command-flags.md`                            | Change the source, run the `bootstrap/gen-*.sh`, commit both. CI runs them with `--check`. |

**11. One format, automated.**
Why: no style arguments in review. Tabs for indentation (shown 4 wide), LF, one final newline, no trailing spaces. Run `bash scripts/format.sh` before every commit; `bash scripts/format.sh --check` is the first thing CI runs, and a failure skips every other job. `git config core.hooksPath .githooks` installs a pre-commit hook that checks it. YAML keeps spaces and Markdown keeps its indentation. `.editorconfig` sets your editor.

## Tests

**9. Tests source `tests/lib/harness.sh` and do not define `fail`, `code` or the temp-dir trap again (ratchet).**
Why: one harness, no copies. `tests/run-all.sh` finds tests by name, and `tests/dry-test.sh` fails when a test file is not listed in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`. See [Tests](/developer/tests/index.html).

## MatchBox

**8. Respect the MatchBox quirks in shared code.**
Why: MatchBox differs from BoxLang on the JVM in ways that crash or silently misbehave.

* No base classes: compose and delegate.
* A class must not `new` its own class (stack overflow at load).
* No closures that call class methods.
* No postfix operators on indexes.
* Build large struct literals stepwise.
* Check a JSON key exists before reading it.
* Never name a variable like a function of the same class: `info = ...` hides `function info`.
* Strings compare case-insensitively with `==`. Compare exact-case keys with `compare()`.

## Documentation of your code

Every function and class in a `.bx` file has a DocBox comment, public or private: a one-sentence summary, `@param` for every argument and `@return`. Tests and generated classes are exempt. See `AGENTS.md` in the repository root, and the example in [Add a command](/developer/add-a-command/index.html).

## Advanced

The existing code is being brought up to the DocBox rule in a pass of its own. Until then, do not leave a function you add or change without its block.

title: Releases and docs
body: Releases and docs This page covers the docs site and the release flow. For code rules see Code rules . The docs are built with bxSites from docs/ and bxsites.yaml , and published to GitHub Pages at https://bxrig.boxlang.io by .github/workflows/docs.yml on every push to development . A pull request builds and audits the site without publishing it. Preview the docs bx-module install bx-sites boxlang bxSites serve # build and serve with live reload boxlang bxSites build # build to site/ boxlang bxSites audit # check the built site, links included Run audit before you open a pull request: CI runs it too. Add or edit a page Put the Markdown file in the section folder where readers will look for it. markdown:
# Releases and docs

This page covers the docs site and the release flow. For code rules see [Code rules](/developer/code-rules/index.html).

The docs are built with [bxSites](https://bxsites.io) from `docs/` and `bxsites.yaml`, and published to GitHub Pages at <https://bxrig.boxlang.io> by `.github/workflows/docs.yml` on every push to `development`. A pull request builds and audits the site without publishing it.

## Preview the docs

```bash
bx-module install bx-sites
boxlang bxSites serve           # build and serve with live reload
boxlang bxSites build           # build to site/
boxlang bxSites audit           # check the built site, links included
```

Run `audit` before you open a pull request: CI runs it too.

## Add or edit a page

1. Put the Markdown file in the section folder where readers will look for it.

2. Start it with frontmatter:

   ```yaml
   ---
   title: Add a command
   order: 83
   summary: One sentence that says what the page helps you do.
   ---
   ```

3. Link to other pages with relative paths (`../build/boxlang.md`), never absolute URLs.

4. Run `boxlang bxSites serve` and look at it.

|   Section    |        Folder        | Order |
|--------------|----------------------|-------|
| Home         | `docs/index.md`      | 1     |
| Start        | `docs/start/`        | 10    |
| Desktop      | `docs/desktop/`      | 20    |
| Customize    | `docs/customize/`    | 30    |
| Build        | `docs/build/`        | 40    |
| AI           | `docs/ai/`           | 50    |
| Data         | `docs/data/`         | 60    |
| Maintain     | `docs/maintain/`     | 70    |
| Developer    | `docs/developer/`    | 80    |
| Reference    | `docs/reference/`    | 90    |
| Architecture | `docs/architecture/` | 100   |

> **Warning:** `docs/reference/commands.md` and `command-flags.md` are generated from `docs/reference/cli.json` by `bootstrap/gen-docs.sh`. Edit `cli.json` and regenerate; never edit those two by hand. See [Add a command](/developer/add-a-command/index.html).

### Writing style

* Lead with what the reader will do. Show the shortest working example first.
* Short paragraphs, numbered steps for tasks, tables for choices.
* Put edge cases and long option tables under an `## Advanced` heading at the bottom.
* Use blockquotes for callouts: `> **Tip:**`, `> **Note:**`, `> **Warning:**`.
* `{{ version }}` and `{{ installUrl }}` are site variables from `bxsites.yaml`.

### Diagrams

Use a fenced `mermaid` block. Keep it small (about ten nodes), label nodes in double quotes, avoid special characters, and put a one-line sentence before it saying what it shows.

````markdown
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["Edit"] --> B["Build"] --> C["Test"]
```
````

### Screenshots and clips

Images live in `docs/assets/screenshots/` (`.webp`) and clips in `docs/assets/clips/` (`.webm`, and `.gif` for places that cannot play video). Name them after the feature: `control-center-dashboard.webp`.

```markdown
![The Control Center dashboard](../assets/screenshots/control-center-dashboard.webp)

<video src="../assets/clips/control-center.webm" poster="../assets/screenshots/control-center-dashboard.webp" autoplay loop muted playsinline width="100%"></video>
```

Always write alt text that says what the picture shows. A clip needs a `poster` screenshot. `tools/record-term.py` records a terminal command for docs and pull requests.

### Links

Every relative link must resolve. `boxlang bxSites audit` finds the broken ones. Fix them before you push.

## Versions

`docs/` is the version being written, **1.0.x**. When it ships, freeze a copy:

```bash
boxlang bxSites version:new --name=1.0.x      # freezes docs/versions/1.0.x
```

Then set `versions.default: "1.0.x"` in `bxsites.yaml`. The release is served at the root and `docs/` becomes `/next/`. Every theme gets a version switcher.

* Patch releases edit `docs/versions/1.0.x/` in place.
* A new minor or major release cuts a new version.

## Languages

English only for now. To add one:

```bash
boxlang bxSites i18n:new --code=es
```

List it under `i18n.locales` in `bxsites.yaml`. `boxlang bxSites i18n:status` reports coverage.

## Releases

|           What you do           |      What ships       |
|---------------------------------|-----------------------|
| Push to `development`           | The `beta` channel.   |
| Push a tag that starts with `v` | The `stable` channel. |

CI builds, signs and publishes the binary and the one-line installer. Users pick a channel with `bxrig update channel`. See [Updates and channels](/maintain/updates/index.html) and [Security](/maintain/security/index.html).

## Advanced

* **Who builds what.** `.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs the tests and the S3 publish job (a `v*` tag publishes under `releases/VERSION`, a `development` push under `snapshots/`). `docs.yml` builds the docs and first runs `bootstrap/gen-docs.sh --check`, so a stale command reference fails the docs build.
* **MatchBox builds.** `scripts/get-matchbox.sh` and `.github/workflows/matchbox.yml` build and publish the MatchBox that BxRig is compiled with.
* **Release signing.** The release key is generated with `scripts/gen-signing-key.sh`; the update flow verifies an Ed25519 signature and the SHA-256 of the binary.

# Design records

These are the long-form records behind BxRig 1.0.x. To build something, start with the [Developer section](/developer/index.html); come here for the why.

* [Command contract](/architecture/COMMAND-CONTRACT/index.html): every command, exit code and file.
* [Shortcut decisions](/architecture/SHORTCUTS-DECISIONS/index.html): two key styles, one table.
* [Desktop decisions](/architecture/DESKTOP-DECISIONS/index.html): top bar, dock, icons, themes.
* [MatchBox parity](/architecture/MATCHBOX-PARITY/index.html) and [port status](/architecture/PORT-STATUS/index.html).

The Mac private key changed in the second round (Cmd+Shift+N) |

## Consequences

* Every hand-written bind (starter `hyprland.lua` and `bxrig.lua`) moves into the one shortcut table, which has a key set per style.
* Mac mode also swaps Alt and Win on PC keyboards (asked in the wizard; Apple keyboard: no swap).
* New runner entries: region record, dictation toggle, color picker, time, battery and weather notices, a Shortcuts section (list, search, rebind, run); second round: recording with audio, quake console, private browser window, file manager here, webcam, and a top-level Hardware section.

## Owner answers to the open questions (2026-11-15)

* Panel keys `Super+Ctrl+A/B/N/P/D` (r18) all open the Noctalia control center panel, the same action as `Super+Alt+C`. No panel ids are needed.
* r25 Mac input language is `Super+Alt+I` and `Super+Alt+Shift+I` (confirmed).
* r39 close window: `Super+Q` closes the window in both styles. Traditional also has `Super+W`. In the Mac style `Super+W` stays the Ctrl+W remap (close tab, which closes the window in most apps).
* r10 `Print` is the region screenshot. Traditional has `Print` only; the Mac style also has `Super+Shift+3/4/5`.
* r31 `Super+Ctrl+Alt+F` ("full screen desktop", a shell toggle that hides the bar) toggles the Noctalia bar in both styles (`appearance bar toggle`). The Mac full screen is `Super+Ctrl+F`, unchanged.
* Workspace moves: Traditional keeps `Super+Shift+1..0`. In the Mac style `Super+Shift+3/4/5` are screenshots, so moving a window to workspaces 3, 4 and 5 is `Super+Alt+Shift+3/4/5` (1, 2 and 6 to 0 stay `Super+Shift+N`). `keys conflicts` is clean in both styles.
* xremap is always installed (copy, paste, cut and select all are remaps in both styles); the wizard no longer ties it to the Mac keys question.
* `Alt+Space` (dictation) is the logical Alt key. With the Mac swap on a PC keyboard it is physically the Win key, the same place as Option on a Mac.
* This is the first version: there is no migration step and no migration code.

## Owner request: toggle the dock (2026-11-15)

`Super+Alt+D` shows or hides the dock in both styles (macOS Cmd+Option+D; with the Alt/Win swap on a PC keyboard it lands on the same physical keys). It runs `bxrig appearance dock toggle`, which is Noctalia's `dock-toggle` IPC command. `keys conflicts` is clean. It is also in the runner under Trigger \> Toggle. macOS's "focus the dock" key (Ctrl+F3) is not possible: Noctalia has no IPC command to focus its dock.

## Toggle top bar (2026-11-17)

`Super+Shift+Space` shows or hides the top bar in both styles. It runs `bxrig appearance bar toggle`, the same command as `Super+Ctrl+Alt+F` (r31, "full screen desktop"), so the bar now has two keys. Row id `bar-toggle`, group Window; in the runner under Trigger \> Toggle \> "Top bar: show or hide". The key is free: `Super+Space` is the runner (r1), `Super+Alt+Space` launches apps (r2), `Super+Ctrl+Shift+Space` is the theme switcher, and `keys conflicts` is clean in both styles.

## Second round: the shortcuts that were missing (owner request, 2026-11-15)

|                Action                 |     Traditional     |         Mac         |             Command             |                                                    Choice                                                    |
|---------------------------------------|---------------------|---------------------|---------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Private browser window                | `Super+Alt+Shift+B` | `Super+Shift+N`     | `browser private`               | Mac is Cmd+Shift+N as in Safari and Chrome; it does not clash (the Mac `Super+N` remap needs no Shift)       |
| File manager in the current directory | `Super+Alt+Shift+F` | `Super+Alt+Shift+F` | `files here`                    | Same key in both styles, no Mac equivalent exists                                                            |
| Quake console, show or hide           | `Super+Shift+Grave` | `Super+Shift+Grave` | `window quake`                  | `Super+Grave` stays the AI shell. `Super+Shift+Grave` was reserved for it in r52 and is the nearest free key |
| Quake console, send the window there  | `Super+Ctrl+Grave`  | `Super+Ctrl+Grave`  | `window quake send`             | `Super+Shift+Grave` is taken by the toggle above; `Super+Ctrl+Grave` is the next free one                    |
| Webcam preview, on or off             | `Super+Ctrl+Alt+V`  | `Super+Ctrl+Alt+V`  | `webcam toggle`                 | V for video, next to the `Super+Ctrl+Alt+T/B/W` notice keys                                                  |
| Hardware menu                         | `Super+Ctrl+H`      | `Super+Ctrl+H`      | `menu open hardware`            |                                                                                                              |
| Screen recording with audio           | `Alt+Print`         | `Alt+Print`         | `record toggle --audio=desktop` | The desktop audio case is bound directly. `--audio=mic` is in the Capture menu                               |

Decisions made while building:

* The private browser is the default web browser (`xdg-settings get default-web-browser`, which `default browser` and the wizard set) started with its private flag: Firefox `--private-window`, Chromium, Brave and Chrome `--incognito`, Edge `--inprivate`. Another browser exits 4 with the list of known ones.
* "Current directory" is the working directory of the focused window's deepest child process (`hyprctl activewindow -j` for the pid, `pgrep -P` down the tree, `/proc/PID/cwd`), else the home folder. The folder opens with `xdg-open`, so the default file manager (`default filemanager`) is used.
* The quake console is the special workspace `qconsole`. `window quake` toggles it, and starts the default terminal there the first time. `window quake send` moves the focused window onto it, silently.
* The webcam preview is `mpv` on `/dev/video0` in its own window class `bxrig-webcam`, which a Hyprland window rule floats at a small size. `webcam toggle` starts it, or ends it when it runs.
* Recording audio: `--audio=desktop` records the monitor of the default sink, `--audio=mic` the default input, both with `wf-recorder -a`. Recording both at once is not built: `wf-recorder` takes one audio source.
* The Hardware section is new and top level. It holds what `Setup > Hardware` held (GPU check, input devices, AirPlay), plus the laptop panel, mirror, brightness, a monitor list and the webcam. There is no BxRig command for audio or bluetooth, so the section has no entry for them (the panels stay on `Super+Ctrl+A` and `Super+Ctrl+B`).

## Class API (written before the code)

One table, two styles, renderers that only read the table. Quirks respected: `compare()` for exact-case strings, `var me = this` before a closure, no closure calls a class method, no `extends`.

    KeyStyle                        // ~/.config/bxrig/keystyle.json: { style: traditional|mac, keyboard: pc|apple, swap: bool }
      read() -> { style, keyboard, swap }     // no file: mac when the xremap unit exists, else traditional; swap defaults to true on a PC keyboard
      swapActive() -> bool                    // style mac AND keyboard pc AND swap on (an Apple keyboard never swaps)
      write( data ) -> exit code              // through JsonStore (config service: backup, journal)

    LuaModule                       // the Lua text both the module and the starter need
      optional( file, var, apply ) -> [lines] // the "load ~/.config/bxrig/theme/FILE.lua if present" block, written once

    Shortcuts( overrides = "", style = "" )   // style: "traditional" | "mac" | a KeyStyle struct; default KeyStyle.read()
      table() -> rows of { id, group, action, kind, keys, keysBy: { traditional, mac }, dispatch, words, opts }
                 kind: remap (xremap) | bind (Hyprland and Plasma) | hypr-bind (Hyprland only); keys "" = no key in this style
      conflicts() -> { within, remapShadows, user }       // table + remaps active in this style + hl.bind lines of your own files
      render( "xremap" | "hyprland" | "plasma" )          // read only the table
      argvOf( id ) -> the bxrig argv a row runs (for `keys run ID`), [] for a pure Lua dispatch

    CLI additions (cli.json): keys style [traditional|mac] [--keyboard=pc|apple] [--swap=on|off] [--yes] | keys search TEXT | keys run ID
                              notify time|battery|weather | screenshot color | dictation toggle | menu open ROUTE

Second round, written before the code. Every new command acts at once (no `--yes`: it changes no file), takes `--dry-run` (prints the argv, exit 0) and `--json`, builds argv arrays only, and exits 0 done, 4 precondition (tool or browser missing), 6 the tool failed.

    Programs( cli, runner = "" )
      privateArgv( desktopId, url ) -> [ program, flag, url? ]   // [] for a browser it does not know
      browserPrivate( url, dryRun, asJson ) -> exit code           // `browser private [URL]`
      cwdOf( pid ) -> path                                        // the deepest child's /proc/PID/cwd
      filesHere( dir, dryRun, asJson ) -> exit code                // `files here [DIR]`

    Webcam( cli, runner = "" )
      argv() -> the mpv argv       running() -> bool
      toggle( dryRun, asJson )     status( asJson )                // `webcam toggle|status`

    Record.start( region, dryRun, asJson, audio = "" )            // audio: "" | desktop | mic
      audioSource( audio ) -> the wf-recorder device name or ""

    MacExtras.window( action, asJson )                            // adds quake and quake-send (`window quake [send]`)
    MenuTree                                                      // a top-level Hardware section (route: hardware)
    Shortcuts rows                                                // browser-private, files-here, quake-toggle, quake-send, webcam, menu-hardware, screen-record-audio
